projects.name: LLM-ProS
projects.title: What can a model solve on its first try?
projects.summary: A zero-shot evaluation of five LLMs on 166 ICPC World Finals problems, using official judge verdicts to examine correctness, error patterns, and temporal performance.
projects.pitch: LLM-ProS benchmarks five models on 166 ICPC World Finals problems in a single-attempt setting. I built the problem collection and submission pipeline and analyzed correctness and failure patterns. The reasoning-oriented o1 models solved 16 and 15 problems; the other three solved none in this setting. The study motivated moving from measuring one-shot capability to testing how execution feedback can help.
ownership: Automated collection and preprocessing of 166 ICPC problems.
Built Codeforces Gym submission and verdict collection.
Analyzed correctness, error types, runtime and memory evidence.
projects.finding: o1-mini: 9.64%; o1-preview: 9.04%. GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B: 0 accepted under this protocol.
projects.caution: Model-family comparisons do not isolate chain-of-thought as a causal factor. Year-based results suggest contamination risk; they do not prove which examples were in training.
projects.next: A-ProS adds repeated execution feedback to this evaluation setting.

projects.name: A-ProS
projects.title: Can useful feedback improve the next attempt?
projects.summary: A generator and a debugging critic work through judge feedback, with persistent conversation context and up to three refinement rounds. Six model pairings are evaluated on 367 problems.
projects.pitch: A-ProS separates writing a solution from diagnosing its failures. We evaluated two generators paired with three critics, on 167 ICPC and 200 Codeforces problems. I built orchestration, submission, verdict logging and the ablation and calibration analyses. On ICPC, GPT-5 workflows went from 39 accepted solutions to 85 to 90 after three refinement rounds. A 47-problem memory ablation showed less verdict repetition, but its solve-rate differences were not statistically conclusive.
ownership: Designed orchestration and implemented Selenium/Playwright automation.
Built verdict capture and SQLite experiment logging.
Conducted context-memory ablations and critic calibration analysis.
projects.finding: Stateful refinement had a descriptive 8.5 to 10.6 percentage-point advantage on 47 matched problems, and 2.9 to 3.5 times lower verdict repetition.
projects.caution: 39 to 90 is out of 167 ICPC problems, not all 367. Memory solve-rate confidence intervals touch zero. More than 2× refers to gains over the initial baseline, not final accuracy.
projects.next: XLAgent moves from isolated contest solutions to defects across repository language boundaries.

projects.name: XLAgent
projects.title: What breaks when two languages meet?
projects.summary: An empirical study and repair framework for Java-TypeScript and Python-Go bugs. It combines a cross-language navigation graph, localization, contract reasoning, editing and isolated evaluation.
projects.pitch: XLAgent studies bugs that require coordinated changes across interacting languages. I carried out the project with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI. We mined 145 repositories, confirmed 86 candidate fixes and retained 31 under a strict definition. The graph connected 11 of 12 in-scope fixes, but did not improve localization over shell search. On five executable bugs, the system edited both developer-file sides more often, but did not establish better repair correctness. The most important lessons concern leakage and the limits of the evaluation oracle.
ownership: Author record: carried out the project independently, with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI.
Built mining, graph navigation, localization/editing and evaluation infrastructure.
Investigated leakage, test coupling, matched controls and narrowed claims.
projects.finding: Developer-file two-sided edits: 4.0 / 5 versus 2.7 for baseline and 3.0 for a matched single agent, averaged across three replicates. Repair correctness did not improve.
projects.caution: Only Python-Go bugs are executable in the repair set. Three of five hidden suites depend on developer-specific names. Graph localization results are null. Manuscript is under review; acceptance is not claimed.
projects.next: A PhD direction: reliable evidence and behavioral oracles for agentic software repair.

questions.question: What is LLM-ProS in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: It is a zero-shot benchmarking framework for five LLMs on 166 ICPC World Finals problems. We submit generated solutions to Codeforces Gym and analyze acceptance and failure verdicts.
detail: LLM-ProS starts from a simple distinction: source code can look convincing without solving the stated problem. An ICPC solution must choose an appropriate algorithm, implement it correctly, handle edge cases and satisfy the resource limits. We therefore evaluate executable solutions through Codeforces Gym rather than asking another model whether the source looks reasonable.

We collected 166 World Finals problems from 2011 through 2024 and evaluated GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Llama-3.1-405B, o1-mini and o1-preview with one candidate per task. o1-mini solved 16 problems, or 9.64%, and o1-preview solved 15, or 9.04%. The other three models solved none under this protocol.

I built problem collection, preprocessing and submission automation and analyzed judge outcomes. The result showed both a model-family difference and substantial remaining difficulty. It did not isolate chain-of-thought as the cause. The low first-attempt success motivated A-ProS: could a model use execution feedback to improve a failed solution?
questions.caution: This is a workshop publication at ICSE 2025 LLM4Code.
followups: Why ICPC?

questions.question: What research question did LLM-ProS address?
questions.answer: We asked how well contemporary LLMs solve difficult algorithmic problems on the first attempt, how performance varies by year and topic, and what failure patterns appear.
detail: I wanted to understand complete algorithmic problem solving rather than just syntactically valid generation. Specifically, we examined first-attempt success on difficult ICPC tasks, variation across years and algorithmic categories, differences among model families and the distribution of failure verdicts. Those questions separate overall capability from the kinds of mistakes a model makes.

We gave each model a problem specification, generated a candidate and used Codeforces Gym to obtain an execution verdict. For example, an accepted solution counts toward first-attempt success, while a compile error and a wrong answer identify different observable failure categories. Grouping those outcomes by year and category reveals patterns hidden by an overall percentage.

The study establishes measured performance under a particular task and prompting protocol. It does not reveal proprietary training data or isolate architecture, training and inference compute. I therefore describe the result as a controlled evaluation of existing systems, with several plausible explanations for the observed differences.
questions.caution: The design compares existing systems; it does not identify their hidden training mechanisms.
followups: What does acceptance actually measure?

questions.question: Why use ICPC World Finals problems?
questions.answer: They require choosing an algorithm, implementing it correctly, handling edge cases and meeting time and memory limits. That makes them a demanding controlled test of program generation.
detail: I chose World Finals problems because they require an entire chain of reasoning: interpret constraints, select an algorithm, implement it and make it survive tests under resource limits. A solution that uses quadratic work where the input requires a near-linear algorithm can fail even when its basic logic seems sensible. This is a stronger test than code that merely compiles.

The tasks have explicit input and output contracts and established judge infrastructure. That gives us consistent acceptance and failure evidence across models. The same problem can expose algorithmic, implementation, formatting and efficiency failures, allowing us to study more than the appearance of the generated code.

ICPC is still a narrow environment. It does not include dependency management, ambiguous user reports, evolving APIs or coordinated changes across a repository. I use it as a demanding controlled testbed, then treat transfer to software maintenance as a separate research question. That distinction is one reason I moved toward XLAgent.
questions.caution: Contest tasks represent a narrow part of software engineering. They do not measure repository maintenance or collaboration.
followups: How would you evaluate repository work instead?

questions.question: Which models and problems were evaluated?
questions.answer: Five models: GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Llama-3.1-405B, o1-mini and o1-preview. The benchmark contains 166 ICPC World Finals problems from 2011 through 2024.
detail: We evaluated GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Llama-3.1-405B, o1-mini and o1-preview on 166 ICPC World Finals problems spanning 2011 through 2024. The comparison deliberately included both general-purpose and reasoning-oriented model families. Each candidate had to satisfy the same task specification and official judge requirements.

For each problem, the model received a preprocessed statement containing the relevant constraints and public examples. It generated one solution without a judge-driven revision loop, and that solution was submitted to Codeforces Gym. We analyzed acceptance, verdict types and the execution information returned by the platform.

These are the models and versions used in the historical study, so I would not substitute newer product names when presenting the result. The study is also not an equal-compute experiment across architectures. Its strongest claim is a performance comparison under the documented protocol, not a current universal ranking of coding ability.
questions.caution: These are historical model results, not a current leaderboard.
followups: Why not compare only models with equal compute?

questions.question: What were the headline results?
questions.answer: o1-mini obtained 16 accepted solutions out of 166, or 9.64%; o1-preview obtained 15, or 9.04%. GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B obtained zero accepted solutions in this setting.
detail: The best observed result was o1-mini with 16 accepted solutions out of 166, or 9.64%. o1-preview had 15, or 9.04%. GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B had no accepted solutions in this first-attempt setting. Reporting the counts matters because the percentage difference between the two o1 models is only one problem.

There are two findings in that result. The reasoning-oriented systems separated themselves from the other tested models, but the absolute success rate remained low. Even the strongest workflow still failed on most World Finals tasks. That makes the benchmark useful for studying failures rather than only celebrating a ranking.

Zero acceptance here does not mean a model is useless at software development, and the model-family gap does not isolate one training mechanism. My conclusion is specific: these tasks remained difficult under one-shot generation, which motivated investigating execution feedback and iterative refinement in A-ProS.
questions.caution: Zero acceptance here does not mean those models cannot write useful code in general.
followups: Does the ranking establish a causal explanation?

questions.question: What is your contribution to LLM-ProS?
questions.answer: I designed the automated problem collection and preprocessing pipeline, built Codeforces Gym submission automation, and analyzed correctness and execution results.
detail: My contribution covered the evaluation infrastructure. I designed the automated collection and preprocessing pipeline for the 166 ICPC problems, built the Codeforces Gym submission pipeline and analyzed the resulting correctness and execution evidence. I can trace the process from an original problem statement to the generated candidate and its recorded verdict.

The pipeline was part of the research method. Losing an inequality during extraction could change the task, and assigning a delayed verdict to the wrong candidate could corrupt the measured success rate. Connecting statements, prompts, generated programs and results made the model comparison and failure analysis possible.

I use I for those concrete implementation and analysis responsibilities, and we for the paper's joint design and findings. LLM-ProS was a collaboration with my coauthors. My claim is that I built and understood the core evaluation machinery, not that I independently performed every contribution to the publication.

questions.question: Walk me through the pipeline.
questions.answer: Collect ICPC statements, extract and validate their components, format prompts, request a model solution, submit to Codeforces Gym, and store verdicts for analysis.
detail: The pipeline begins by collecting ICPC World Finals problems and extracting the statement, input and output specification, constraints, examples and limits. We clean the extracted content and check that the prompt still represents the original task. This is essential because a corrupted constraint can turn the evaluation into a different problem.

We format the task for each model, generate a candidate and submit the program to Codeforces Gym. The platform compiles and executes it under its test suite and resource limits. The resulting verdict tells us whether that particular candidate was accepted, not merely whether it looked plausible.

We then aggregate acceptance and failure verdicts by model, year and category. I keep the interpretation at the level of the recorded evidence: a compile error, wrong answer and submission infrastructure failure are different events. A trustworthy pipeline must preserve that distinction before a numerical comparison is meaningful.
questions.caution: The latter separation is an evaluation practice to check in logs, not an extra reported result.
followups: Where could the pipeline introduce bias?

questions.question: How did you preprocess problem statements?
questions.answer: We extracted statements, input and output specifications, examples, notes and limits, then cleaned encoding and formatting and manually checked the resulting prompts.
detail: We extracted the statement into its functional parts: the task, input format, output format, constraints, samples, notes and resource limits. We then cleaned encoding and formatting and manually checked the resulting prompts. The aim was to preserve meaning, not simply produce tidy text.

A PDF parser can drop a superscript, reverse an inequality or scramble a table. For instance, losing a large input bound can make an infeasible algorithm look appropriate. Mathematical notation and examples therefore need comparison against the original source, especially when a failure might otherwise be blamed on the model.

I would create an extraction checklist and a reviewed sample with explicit categories of errors, then measure how often each occurs. That would distinguish model failure from task-corruption failure. The study documents preprocessing and manual review; a formal extraction-error audit would be a stronger follow-up rather than a result I claim we already measured.
questions.caution: A clean-looking prompt can still be semantically incomplete.
followups: How would you test extraction quality?

questions.question: What does zero-shot mean in this study?
questions.answer: The model receives the problem specification without worked training examples for that task and generates its first solution without iterative judge feedback.
detail: Zero-shot means that the model receives the problem specification and produces its first candidate without task-specific worked demonstrations or iterative judge feedback. The public sample input and output remain part of the specification. They explain the problem and are not additional demonstrations of the hidden solution algorithm.

The model sees the formatted statement, generates a program and that program is judged. There is no step in LLM-ProS where a failed submission is returned to a critic for another attempt. That later feedback loop is the central difference in A-ProS.

Zero-shot describes what we put in the prompt; it says nothing definitive about pretraining exposure. A model might previously have encountered an old problem or solution. I therefore do not use zero-shot as a synonym for unseen or uncontaminated. Those claims require separate evidence about task release dates and model training exposure.
questions.caution: Distinguish prompt setup from training contamination.
followups: Is zero-shot the same as uncontaminated?

questions.question: What does pass@1 measure here?
questions.answer: The fraction of benchmark problems whose first generated candidate is accepted by the judge under this protocol.
detail: In this study, pass@1 is the fraction of benchmark problems whose first generated candidate receives an accepted verdict. For o1-mini the calculation is 16 divided by 166, giving approximately 9.64%. Each task contributes one first-attempt outcome under the documented protocol.

A model given several independent samples or several feedback-driven revisions has more opportunities to solve a task. Its eventual success rate answers a different question. I would therefore report first-attempt acceptance separately from success after a four-submission loop, even if both are expressed as percentages.

A judge pass is evidence that a candidate satisfied that test suite and its resource limits. It is not formal proof over every possible input. The metric also depends on a valid submission and task-processing pipeline, so I would not silently count an authentication timeout as a program failure.
questions.caution: Finite tests and harness correctness bound what acceptance establishes.
followups: How is pass@k different?

questions.question: Why use an external judge?
questions.answer: It evaluates programs against a stable task-specific test suite and resource limits, reducing reliance on subjective inspection of source code.
detail: An external judge executes the program against task-specific tests and resource limits. That is stronger evidence than an evaluator saying the code resembles a correct solution. A candidate must produce the required output and do so without violating the contest's execution constraints.

The verdict categories include acceptance, wrong answer, compile error, runtime error, time-limit failure and memory-limit failure. These distinguish several observable ways generation can fail. Runtime and memory information can also inform the efficiency analysis, provided the platform and comparison conditions are understood.

The judge is not an unlimited correctness oracle. Tests may miss cases, and an incorrect wrapper, language selection or extraction can create a misleading outcome. I treat the judge as a reproducible measurement instrument that still needs a valid environment. That same lesson became especially important for XLAgent's one-sided and implementation-coupled tests.
questions.caution: Acceptance is not a proof of correctness for all possible inputs.
followups: What can a judge miss?

questions.question: What can go wrong in browser submission automation?
questions.answer: Authentication, dynamic pages, delayed verdicts, language selection and retries can all corrupt the mapping from candidate to result.
detail: Browser automation can fail before the program is evaluated: the session may expire, the page may change, a language option may be wrong or the verdict may still be pending. The dangerous case is not only a visible crash. It is a plausible-looking result attached to the wrong problem or candidate.

I would give every attempt a stable task and candidate identifier, record the external submission ID and wait for a terminal verdict. After a timeout, I would reconcile whether the platform accepted the submission before sending another one. This prevents accidental duplicates from consuming the attempt budget.

Infrastructure outcomes need their own status and retry policy rather than becoming wrong-answer verdicts. My recorded contribution includes browser submission and verdict collection. The safeguards I have described are the design principles I would defend and check against the actual implementation, rather than claiming an undocumented historical recovery mechanism.
questions.caution: The reliability design is prospective. Historical implementation guarantees require checking the actual code and logs.

followups: How would you make retries idempotent?

questions.question: Were prompts exactly identical across models?
questions.answer: The paper uses standardized problem components with some model-specific template adjustments, including additional reasoning guidance for the o1 family.
detail: The paper standardizes the core problem components but also describes model-specific template adjustments, including extra reasoning guidance for the o1 family. That helps accommodate the models, but it means the comparison changes both the model family and some aspects of prompting.

If one configuration performs better, the difference could reflect model capability, prompt compatibility or their interaction. The observed ranking is still useful, but it does not identify training methodology alone as the cause. That is why I avoid describing the result as a clean chain-of-thought intervention.

I would cross each model with a small set of matched prompt templates, including direct generation and a common reasoning instruction where supported. I would preserve the same tasks and account for inference budgets. That would show whether the model-family gap remains stable across prompts and whether a particular template disproportionately helps one family.
questions.caution: Do not describe the comparison as isolating model training alone.
followups: What matched control would you add?

questions.question: What information should be logged for reproducibility?
questions.answer: The exact task, prompt, model identifier, configuration, generated source, submission identifier and verdict should be retained.
detail: A reproducible record should link the exact task, prompt, requested and returned model identity, configuration, generated program, submission ID and terminal verdict. I would also retain timestamps and the raw response or error information needed to reconstruct how the summary was produced.

A result table alone cannot show whether two rows refer to the same candidate, whether a retry created another sample or whether an API alias changed during the study. Stable IDs and content hashes make those questions auditable. The analysis should derive its aggregates from the retained attempt records.

Even an excellent archive may not reproduce identical outputs from a model API years later. It can still reproduce the analysis and let someone inspect the evidence behind the original result. I distinguish those goals: reproducing an observed table is different from recreating the exact stochastic behavior of a retired or changed model.

questions.question: Does this prove chain-of-thought caused the better performance?
questions.answer: No. The reasoning-oriented model families performed better, but architecture, training data, compute and prompt differences were not independently controlled.
detail: No. The reasoning-oriented models performed better in our experiment, but we did not independently vary chain-of-thought while holding architecture, training data and inference compute fixed. We also used some model-specific prompt adjustments. Those factors can contribute to the observed performance gap.

The measured result is that o1-mini and o1-preview obtained accepted solutions where the three other tested systems did not, under the documented protocol. That is consistent with reasoning-oriented systems being useful on these tasks. It is not enough to attribute the difference to one hidden training mechanism.

I would compare closely matched models or controlled inference interventions, use the same tasks and prompts where possible, and report the compute budget. If the gain persisted under those controls, the causal interpretation would become stronger. For this paper, I keep the empirical ranking separate from the proposed explanation.

questions.question: Did you prove dataset contamination?
questions.answer: No. Temporal performance patterns raise a contamination concern, but a year-based split cannot reveal the contents of proprietary training data.
detail: No. We compared performance across problem years, including a 2024 subset treated as temporally held out under the stated training-cutoff assumptions. That raises a useful contamination question, but it does not reveal whether a proprietary model actually saw a specific statement or solution during training.

Older and newer contest years can differ in difficulty and category mix, and the annual subsets are small. A lower result on one year could arise without memorization. Likewise, solving a new problem does not prove the model never encountered a related algorithm or reformulation.

I would combine a prospectively collected task stream with release-date records, solution-similarity audits and controlled transformations. Even then, the wording should match what is known. The conclusion I defend from LLM-ProS is that temporal evaluation is important and contamination is a threat, not that we established a definitive contamination rate.
questions.caution: Do not call the benchmark proven contamination-free.
followups: What stronger contamination audit is possible?

questions.question: Why did three models score zero?
questions.answer: The data show their candidates failed the judge under this demanding first-attempt setup. A breakdown of verdicts helps identify compilation, runtime and semantic failures.
detail: GPT-4o, Mistral Large and Llama-3.1-405B had no accepted candidates in our first-attempt World Finals setting. Their failures were not all the same. Table II includes compilation, runtime, time-limit and wrong-answer outcomes, so the zero total combines several different problems.

GPT-4o has 41 compile errors and 55 wrong answers in the reported table. A compile error can involve invalid generated source or an interface mismatch with the execution setup. A wrong answer means the program ran but did not satisfy the judge. Those outcomes call for different investigation.

The result alone cannot identify one cause such as lack of reasoning or memorization. Prompt compatibility and task difficulty are potential contributors. I interpret zero acceptance as a bounded result of this evaluation protocol, not a statement that those systems cannot produce useful code or improve when given feedback.
questions.caution: A zero count does not identify one underlying cause.
followups: Would feedback help them?

questions.question: Can you generalize these results to software engineering?
questions.answer: Only cautiously. Contest programs have self-contained specifications and strong judges; maintenance work has dependencies, ambiguous reports, evolving interfaces and multiple files.
detail: The methodological lesson transfers: evaluate executable behavior, preserve the task specification and analyze failures rather than relying on source appearance. Those principles are useful for software agents well beyond contest programming. They also informed the orchestration and measurement work in my later projects.

World Finals tasks are self-contained and have explicit input/output requirements. Repository maintenance introduces dependencies, incomplete bug reports, multiple components and changes that must preserve existing behavior. A success percentage on one setting therefore cannot be treated as evidence of the same success rate on the other.

I moved toward the harder setting rather than claiming the gap was already solved. XLAgent studies interaction defects across repository languages and separates localization, patch shape and behavioral correctness. That progression reflects the limits of the earlier benchmark: it motivates a new experiment instead of allowing us to generalize a contest result by assertion.
questions.caution: Cross-project progression does not make their numerical scores directly comparable.
followups: Why is repository repair harder?

questions.question: How would you improve the study now?
questions.answer: Add budget-matched prompts, multiple independent samples, a stronger temporal protocol, validated extraction and detailed semantic failure labels.
detail: I would strengthen the fairness and validity controls before simply adding more models. I would validate extraction against original statements, compare matched prompt templates, record exact model versions and collect several independent candidate samples under explicit resource budgets. That would separate sampling variability from systematic workflow differences.

I would establish a prospective task collection protocol and stratify results by difficulty and category, while showing counts and uncertainty for each temporal group. I would also annotate a sample of semantic failures, so wrong-answer totals become explanations rather than just outcome labels.

These changes would test whether the observed model-family ranking survives stronger controls and whether the failure patterns predict what kind of feedback is useful. They are proposed improvements. questions.question: What did LLM-ProS teach you?
questions.answer: A working evaluation pipeline is a research instrument. A polished-looking solution is weak evidence; judged outcomes reveal failures, and the evaluation itself still needs validation.
detail: LLM-ProS taught me that the evaluation pipeline is itself a research instrument. A convincing explanation or plausible program is weak evidence if it fails under the actual specification. At the same time, a failure verdict is only useful when the task extraction, submission and judging process are trustworthy.

The low first-attempt acceptance made me interested in what information could help a model revise. A-ProS therefore tested an iterative generator-critic workflow rather than just adding another static ranking. I wanted to understand whether preserving failure evidence changes refinement behavior.

XLAgent then exposed a further issue: even a passing test can be insufficient when it checks only one side of an interaction. Across the projects, my focus shifted from collecting model outputs to asking what each measurement actually establishes. That is the methodological direction I want to deepen through a PhD.
questions.caution: Present this as a research lesson, not an additional empirical result.
followups: How did this change your next project?

questions.question: What is A-ProS in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: A-ProS is an inference-time programming workflow: a generator writes code, a judge evaluates it, and a separate critic diagnoses failures so the generator can revise with context.
detail: A-ProS treats solving as an iterative process. A generator writes a C++ candidate, the judge evaluates it, and a separate critic examines a failure and proposes a targeted hint. The generator then revises the code while preserving the relevant conversation history. The loop stops on acceptance or after four submissions.

We compared six generator-critic pairings on 367 problems: 167 ICPC tasks and 200 Codeforces tasks. On ICPC, GPT-5 workflows moved from 39 initial accepts to 85 through 90 after three feedback rounds. My work covered orchestration, browser automation, verdict logging, context ablations and calibration analysis.

Feedback and memory are useful things to measure, but the details matter. The 47-problem memory study showed lower repeated-verdict rates and a directional solve-rate benefit, without statistically conclusive solve-rate evidence. A-ProS changes inference-time context, not model weights. I describe it as an evaluated workflow, not a newly trained model.
questions.caution: It does not update model weights during the loop.
followups: How is it different from LLM-ProS?

questions.question: How does A-ProS extend LLM-ProS?
questions.answer: LLM-ProS measures a first attempt. A-ProS studies whether judge evidence, a specialized critic and persistent interaction can improve subsequent attempts.
detail: LLM-ProS asks whether a model solves a problem on its first attempt. A-ProS asks what happens after that attempt fails: can execution evidence, a separate debugging role and retained history help the generator produce a better candidate? That is a shift from capability measurement toward studying a problem-solving process.

Instead of ending after a judge verdict, we capture the available diagnostics, obtain a critic's hint and return the evidence to the generator. We record the complete trajectory, so we can examine eventual acceptance, repeated failures and the relationship between critic confidence and the next revision.

The papers use different models and task collections. I therefore would not subtract their success rates and call the difference an effect of A-ProS. The controlled questions are inside A-ProS, such as the stateful versus stateless comparison on matched problems. The progression between papers is conceptual and methodological.

questions.question: What is the 2 by 3 factorial design?
questions.answer: Two generators, GPT-4 and GPT-5, are each paired separately with Codestral-2508, Llama-3.3-70B and DeepSeek-R1 as debugging critics, giving six workflows.
detail: The generator is either GPT-4 or GPT-5. For each generator, we separately test Codestral-2508, Llama-3.3-70B and DeepSeek-R1 as the debugging critic. Two choices multiplied by three choices gives six workflows. A single run uses one generator and one critic, not all three critics voting together.

Holding a generator fixed lets us compare the observed performance under different critics. Holding a critic fixed lets us compare generator tiers. That is useful because an apparent debugging benefit could otherwise come from simply choosing a stronger generator.

The design does not by itself isolate the value of model heterogeneity. A same-model generator-critic control is needed to ask whether using different models helps beyond separating the roles. I would add that comparison with matched tasks, feedback access and inference budgets before claiming a causal benefit from diversity.

questions.question: Why separate generation from criticism?
questions.answer: The roles have different jobs: synthesis must produce an executable solution, while criticism should diagnose the failure and suggest a targeted revision.
detail: Generating a complete program and diagnosing why it failed are related but distinct tasks. The generator must implement the solution, while the critic should connect the failure evidence to a specific change. The separation makes the diagnosis explicit rather than asking for an unrelated fresh sample.

We can change the critic while keeping the generator fixed and inspect the hints associated with later revisions. That exposes whether a critic gives actionable feedback, repeats an incorrect diagnosis or expresses confidence that does not match subsequent outcomes. The role boundary also makes those artifacts easier to log.

The architecture is a hypothesis about useful organization, not proof that two models are always better than one. A fair test also needs self-revision, same-model criticism and budget-matched alternatives. In the published study I defend the observed six-workflow results and the memory analysis, rather than attributing every gain to role separation alone.
questions.caution: Role separation alone does not prove multi-model superiority.
followups: Could one model do both jobs?

questions.question: What exactly reaches the critic?
questions.answer: The problem specification, failed candidate and available execution diagnostics, such as verdict and accessible failing-test information.
detail: The critic receives the problem specification, the failed candidate and the execution evidence available for that task. That can include the verdict and accessible test diagnostics. questions.question: What does persistent context preserve?
questions.answer: Earlier conversational turns for the current task, including previous candidates, failures and feedback, within the relevant generator and critic sessions.
detail: Persistent context preserves earlier conversational turns for the current problem, including prior candidates, failure evidence and debugging advice within the relevant role sessions. The generator and critic can each retain their own conversation. The system is not updating weights or creating a shared learned memory across unrelated tasks.

Suppose one revision fixes a wrong answer but introduces excessive complexity. That gives a concrete mechanism to investigate: using accumulated evidence to avoid cycling.

I would therefore compare full history with compact evidence summaries under matched budgets before claiming that more context is always better.

questions.answer: Solution generation and refinement are model-driven, but the paper describes manual retrieval for some restricted ICPC test diagnostics.

questions.question: Is A-ProS reinforcement learning or RLHF?
questions.answer: No. The evaluated loop changes prompts and context during inference, without updating model parameters.
detail: A-ProS is an inference-time workflow. After a failure, it changes the evidence and instructions in the next prompt, while retaining context where configured. It does not calculate gradients or update the generator's or critic's weights during the loop. That makes it different from reinforcement learning and RLHF training.

A fixed model can produce a different answer when it sees a failed candidate, the judge result and a concrete diagnosis. The improvement comes from conditioning on additional task evidence, not from learning a new parameterized policy between submissions. That distinction is important when interpreting the word adaptation.

I could study a trained policy for choosing critics, stopping or selecting feedback. That would require a separate training protocol, reward definition and held-out evaluation. It is a potential research direction, not something I would describe as already implemented by the A-ProS experiments.
questions.caution: Calling every feedback loop reinforcement learning confuses inference with training.
followups: How could an RL policy extend this?

questions.question: What does SQLite logging contribute scientifically?
questions.answer: It links each task, candidate, hint and judge outcome across attempts, enabling trajectory analysis and paired comparisons instead of only final totals.
detail: SQLite logging connects each task to its candidate attempts, critic hints and judge outcomes. That turns an iterative system into an analyzable sequence. Without that structure, a final accepted count would not show how many attempts were used or what evidence preceded a revision.

The memory study needs matched task outcomes, and calibration needs each confidence value paired with the immediately following generator result. Verdict-repetition analysis also depends on the correct ordering of attempts. Those are relational questions, so structured identifiers are more useful than a folder of unconnected text files.

A database is not automatically trustworthy just because it is structured. I would validate missing attempts, duplicates and candidate-to-submission mappings and preserve raw artifacts. My contribution includes the logging infrastructure; specific schema constraints or recovery guarantees should be checked in the implementation before I claim that they were enforced historically.
questions.caution: Inspect the actual schema before claiming a particular constraint or recovery policy.

questions.question: Why does feedback sometimes make the solution worse?
questions.answer: A revision can fix one issue while creating another, or a critic can give an incorrect diagnosis. Acceptance is not guaranteed to improve monotonically along a single trajectory.
detail: The critic may diagnose the wrong cause, or the generator may implement a good hint incorrectly. A revision can also fix one property while breaking another. Correctness and efficiency are coupled, so improving an edge case does not guarantee the new algorithm meets the resource limit.

The paper's Sums on Segments example for GPT-4 with DeepSeek goes from Wrong Answer to Time Limit Exceeded, then Wrong Answer and finally Accepted. That is not a monotonic improvement in every intermediate outcome. It illustrates why the complete trajectory is more informative than only the successful endpoint.

I would retain each candidate and test what changed, then distinguish harmful advice from implementation errors and new regressions. The worked example is an illustration, not an estimate of how often regression occurs. A stronger study would label a representative sample of trajectories and compare feedback policies against that annotation.

followups: How could the loop reject harmful hints?

questions.question: Why are algorithmic tags not disjoint?
questions.answer: A problem may require several techniques, such as graphs and dynamic programming, so it can appear in multiple category counts.
detail: Algorithmic categories describe techniques rather than mutually exclusive classes. A single problem can require a graph representation, dynamic programming and arithmetic reasoning. Counting it in each relevant category is legitimate, but summing those category counts does not recover the number of unique benchmark tasks.

If graph problems perform better than geometry problems, the groups may differ in difficulty and may share tasks. That prevents a simple causal claim that a critic specializes in one technique. I would inspect task composition and compare matched workflow outcomes within each group.

I would show the unique task denominator and make overlap explicit in table captions. For statistical analysis, the unit remains the problem, with dependence accounted for rather than treating every category occurrence as a new independent observation. This avoids inflating the sample size through multiple tags.
questions.caution: Do not sum overlapping tags into a benchmark size.
followups: How would you compare performance by category?

questions.question: What did the 47-problem memory study show?
questions.answer: GPT-5 with DeepSeek reached 19 of 47 statefully versus 14 statelessly; GPT-4 reached 12 versus 8. That is a 10.6 and 8.5 percentage-point advantage.
detail: The ablation used 47 problems. GPT-5 with DeepSeek started at 10 solves, then finished at 19 with stateful context and 14 statelessly. GPT-4 started at 5 and finished at 12 versus 8. The stateful advantages are therefore 5 and 4 tasks, or about 10.6 and 8.5 percentage points.

For GPT-5, repeated failure-verdict frequency was 11.8% statefully and 41.8% statelessly. For GPT-4 it was 14.2% versus 40.8%. That is evidence of different refinement behavior when history is retained. The metric counts verdict categories, not independently diagnosed semantic mistakes.

The raw McNemar p-values were 0.063 and 0.125, and the reported bootstrap intervals touched zero. I describe the solve-rate differences as directional evidence on a small set, not a statistically conclusive memory benefit. A larger matched study is needed before making a stronger acceptance claim.
questions.caution: The solve-rate effects are descriptive and statistically inconclusive.
followups: What were the p-values?

questions.answer: No. Raw exact McNemar p-values are 0.063 and 0.125, and the reported bootstrap confidence intervals touch zero.

questions.question: What does 3.5 times less error repetition mean?
questions.answer: For GPT-5, the reported repetition rate is 41.8% stateless versus 11.8% stateful; their ratio is about 3.5. GPT-4 gives about 2.9.
detail: For GPT-5 with DeepSeek, the stateless repeated-verdict rate is 41.8% and the stateful rate is 11.8%. Dividing them gives approximately 3.5. GPT-4's 40.8% divided by 14.2% is approximately 2.9. The claim is about the ratio of these observed repetition rates.

A repetition occurs when a feedback iteration produces the same failure verdict category as the previous attempt. For example, Wrong Answer followed by Wrong Answer counts as repetition. Wrong Answer followed by Time Limit Exceeded does not, even though the candidate still fails.

Two wrong answers can come from different bugs, while a changed verdict can reflect a harmful new defect. I therefore treat verdict repetition as a behavioral proxy, not proof that the same reasoning mistake was avoided. To test that stronger mechanism, I would independently label the underlying causes in sampled trajectories.
questions.caution: These measures do not equate repeated verdicts with independently identified repeated reasoning mistakes.
followups: What annotation would measure repeated semantic mistakes?

questions.answer: It compares improvement over the initial baseline. GPT-5 gains 9 stateful solves versus 4 stateless solves, giving 2.25 times the gain; GPT-4 gains 7 versus 3, giving 2.33.

The final GPT-5 totals are 19 and 14, whose ratio is about 1.36. The final GPT-4 totals are 12 and 8, whose ratio is 1.50. Saying final accuracy doubled would therefore misstate what the calculation measures.

I would say that the observed improvement above the starting point was more than twice as large in the stateful condition on this small matched set. I would immediately retain the ablation's uncertainty: solve-rate intervals touch zero and the comparisons are not statistically conclusive. Reexpressing an effect as a ratio does not remove that limitation.

questions.question: Is DeepSeek conclusively the best critic?
questions.answer: It has the best observed results in these comparisons, but individual critic-pair differences were not significant after multiplicity correction.
detail: DeepSeek produced the best observed critic results across the reported pairings. That is a descriptive statement about the experiment. It is different from concluding that DeepSeek is always the best critic or that every individual difference is statistically reliable.

The paper's paired comparisons use McNemar's test, bootstrap differences and multiplicity correction. The individual critic-pair differences do not survive that correction as significant results. Generator-tier differences have stronger reported support, but their significance cannot be transferred to the critic ranking.

I could use the ranking to choose a baseline or form a routing hypothesis, then evaluate that policy separately. I would not assume it will generalize to another task distribution or model version. A good next experiment would compare critics under the same generator, task information and total budget, with enough independent problems to distinguish the relevant effect.

questions.question: What is verification cost in the tables?
questions.answer: Total judge submissions across all tasks divided by the number of accepted solutions, including submissions spent on tasks that remain unsolved.
detail: Verification cost is total judge submissions divided by the number of accepted solutions. It includes submissions spent on problems the workflow never solves. That makes it a measure of how much judging work is consumed per successful task, rather than the average length of successful trajectories alone.

Suppose a workflow cheaply solves several easy tasks but repeatedly submits failures on the rest. Ignoring the failed tasks would make the system appear more efficient than it is. Counting all submissions preserves the cost of unsuccessful search.

It is not the monetary price of model calls, total token usage or wall-clock time. Stateful histories and critic calls can make two equal-submission workflows quite different in actual expense. For a deployment decision, I would report those costs separately and compare success under a fixed resource budget rather than treating verification cost as a complete efficiency measure.
questions.caution: Read the table caption before comparing cost metrics.
followups: What other costs should be reported?

questions.question: Can you explain critic calibration?
questions.answer: We ask for confidence from 1 to 5, map it to 0.2 to 1.0 and compare that confidence with whether the immediately following revision is accepted.
detail: We ask the critic for confidence on a scale from 1 to 5 and divide that value by 5. We compare the resulting confidence with acceptance on the immediately following generator attempt. The question is whether confident advice predicts a successful next revision, not simply whether the critic sounds persuasive.

For each confidence bin, calculate the absolute gap between mean stated confidence and observed next-attempt success. Weight the gap by the fraction of hints in that bin and add across bins. A large gap means expressed confidence and observed outcomes do not agree.

The outcome depends on both roles: a good hint may be implemented badly, and a passing program does not certify every sentence of the diagnosis. The scale also cannot express less than 20% confidence. I therefore interpret ECE as calibration of the hint-and-revision outcome, not a pure semantic accuracy score for the critic.
questions.caution: Acceptance is a proxy for hint utility, not a direct label that the entire diagnosis was correct.
followups: Why is the confidence floor a problem?

questions.question: What did the calibration results imply?
questions.answer: All tested pairings had reported ECE above 0.35. DeepSeek was relatively better calibrated, but none should be trusted just because it expresses confidence.
detail: The reported ECE values exceed 0.35 for all tested pairings. DeepSeek is relatively better calibrated than the other critics, but that does not mean its confidence is reliable in absolute terms. The finding argues against accepting a hint solely because the model expresses high certainty.

Hints are issued after a candidate has already failed, so the evaluated population is conditional on difficulty. The 1-to-5 scale also maps the lowest confidence to 0.2, even when next-attempt success can be much rarer. Both affect how the gaps should be interpreted.

I would compare more flexible probability elicitation, held-out recalibration and a routing or abstention policy. The policy would need its own evaluation against fixed-critic baselines under equal cost. The current paper motivates confidence-aware decision making; it does not establish that calibration-based routing was already implemented and improved acceptance.
questions.caution: Calibration-based routing is proposed future work, not a proven component of A-ProS.

questions.question: How would you explain ECE with numbers?
questions.answer: Imagine twenty hints all assigned confidence 4 on the five-point scale. Dividing by five gives predicted confidence 0.8. If only four immediately following revisions are accepted, observed success in that bin is 4 divided by 20, or 0.2. The absolute calibration gap is therefore 0.6.
detail: Imagine twenty hints all assigned confidence 4 on the five-point scale. Dividing by five gives predicted confidence 0.8. If only four immediately following revisions are accepted, observed success in that bin is 4 divided by 20, or 0.2. The absolute calibration gap is therefore 0.6.

If those twenty hints make up one quarter of all hints, that bin contributes 0.25 multiplied by 0.6, or 0.15, to ECE. I repeat that calculation for each bin and sum the contributions. This makes the weighting explicit rather than treating every confidence level as equally frequent.

High confidence can coexist with low practical success. The calculation is illustrative, not another experimental result. ECE also depends on binning and can hide differences across tasks or groups, so I would inspect reliability plots and complementary measures rather than relying on one summary number.

questions.question: Could persistent context simply use more compute?
questions.answer: Yes, retained history can increase input tokens even when submission counts match. An equal-attempt study does not fully control compute or monetary cost.
detail: Yes. Preserving full interaction history generally adds input tokens. Even if both conditions receive four judge submissions, the stateful condition may consume more model context and money. Equal attempts establish one form of budget matching, not complete equal-compute matching.

I would test full history, a compact evidence summary, latest feedback alone and selected retrieved history under the same total token or monetary budget. I would count critic calls and unsuccessful tasks, and measure both final acceptance and whether important earlier failures are forgotten.

The paper provides a specific stateful-versus-stateless comparison and shows a behavioral difference in verdict repetition. It leaves room for cost and information-content explanations. My conclusion is that persistent context is a promising mechanism to investigate, not that the experiment proves unlimited history is the most efficient way to improve refinement.
questions.caution: That is a proposed follow-up; the published result does not settle it.
followups: What is the appropriate budget for deployment?

questions.question: What was the hardest engineering challenge?
questions.answer: The most difficult part of the work I can substantiate was making the iterative experiment trustworthy across several moving components. A generated candidate, browser submission, delayed verdict, critic response and later revision all have to stay connected to the same problem and attempt sequence. A mismatch can invalidate an otherwise convincing trace.

A generated candidate, browser submission, delayed verdict, critic response and later revision all have to stay connected to the same problem and attempt sequence. A mismatch can invalidate an otherwise convincing trace.

I built orchestration, submission automation, verdict capture and SQLite logging so those stages could be observed and analyzed. This infrastructure supported the context ablation and calibration analysis, both of which depend on correct relationships between successive attempts.

Reliability in research automation is not only about keeping the script running. It is about knowing whether the recorded evidence measures the intended event. I would show the actual state transitions and stored artifacts if asked for detail, rather than inventing an anecdote about one particular failure that is not in my records.

questions.question: What are the biggest limitations of A-ProS?
questions.answer: Narrow contest tasks, a small memory ablation, expensive context, uncertain critic reliability and dependence on access to useful execution feedback.
detail: The tasks are competitive programming problems, so the study does not establish broad repository-maintenance ability. The memory ablation contains only 47 matched tasks and its solve-rate differences are statistically inconclusive. The factorial comparison also does not isolate the benefit of heterogeneous models against a same-model critic control.

Longer histories consume more tokens and can retain incorrect advice. Critics are poorly calibrated in the reported analysis, and access to detailed execution evidence is not uniform across all tasks. Some ICPC diagnostic retrieval required human handling, which qualifies the autonomy claim.

I would prioritize a budget-matched feedback study with stronger controls and behaviorally labeled trajectories. For transfer to maintenance, I would separately evaluate repository tasks and their oracles. The useful conclusion is that iterative evidence can be studied systematically, while success, cost and feedback reliability must each be measured rather than assumed.
questions.caution: State limitations with their consequences rather than listing generic threats.
followups: Which one matters most for your PhD work?

questions.question: Would a same-model critic work just as well?
questions.answer: It might. I would add same-model generator-critic controls under the same task, prompt and total budget to isolate whether model diversity contributes beyond role separation.
detail: A same-model critic could plausibly perform as well. The generator and critic roles can be separated even when they use the same underlying model. A-ProS compares several heterogeneous pairings, but that design alone cannot tell whether model diversity contributes beyond the prompting and feedback loop.

I would compare heterogeneous criticism, same-model criticism, verdict-only self-revision and fresh resampling on the same problems. I would match access to diagnostics and account for the total inference budget, not merely the number of submitted programs. The same initial candidates would make feedback effects easier to identify.

The primary measure would be final acceptance under the budget, with secondary labels for diagnosis accuracy, harmful advice and repeated semantic errors. If same-model criticism matches the heterogeneous workflow, the practical lesson would be to prefer the simpler or cheaper design. A negative diversity result would still clarify what makes the workflow useful.

questions.question: How would you improve memory?
questions.answer: Replace raw history with an evidence ledger of attempted hypotheses, changed code, verdicts and unresolved constraints, then compare it with full context under equal cost.
detail: I would replace raw history with an evidence ledger recording attempted hypotheses, relevant code changes, verdicts and unresolved constraints. The aim is to preserve what the system has learned about the current problem without repeatedly replaying every conversational token. This is a proposed extension, not a completed A-ProS result.

I would compare the ledger with full history, latest-feedback-only prompting and selective retrieval under matched total cost. Each condition would use the same tasks and initial candidates. I would also test whether the summary accidentally drops a constraint or converts an uncertain diagnosis into an asserted fact.

I would require comparable or better acceptance and fewer repeated semantic mistakes at lower cost, not merely a shorter prompt. If summaries lose essential evidence, the result would show where compact memory needs richer structure. That makes the proposal falsifiable rather than assuming that compression automatically improves reasoning.

questions.question: How would you test whether a hint is actually useful?
questions.answer: Hold the task and candidate fixed, randomly assign a real hint, a shuffled hint, verdict-only feedback or no hint, then compare matched revisions.
detail: I would hold the failed candidate and task fixed, then randomly assign the next revision to receive the real hint, a shuffled hint from another task, verdict-only feedback or no hint. This separates useful diagnostic content from the benefit of another generation opportunity or simply asking the model to try again.

The generator, sampling settings, available specification and total budget would remain comparable. I would collect several revisions per task while preserving the task as the independent unit. Reviewers could separately label whether each diagnosis is correct and whether the generator follows it.

Acceptance is the primary practical outcome, but I would also examine harmful changes and semantic error recurrence. A real hint beating both shuffled advice and verdict-only revision would provide stronger evidence of diagnostic usefulness. This is a proposed causal study; the existing next-attempt calibration measure does not establish that entire mechanism.
questions.caution: An immediate accepted revision alone cannot establish that every hint was correct.
followups: Why include a shuffled-hint control?

questions.question: How would you reduce cost without losing reliability?
questions.answer: Test early stopping, compact history and critic escalation under a fixed budget, and report a cost-success frontier instead of only the best accuracy.
detail: I would start with compact evidence and a low-cost critic, escalating only when an independently validated signal suggests another round is worth the expense. I would also test early stopping and history compression. The objective would be useful success under a fixed budget rather than maximizing attempts regardless of cost.

Each policy would run on the same tasks and initial candidates. I would include fixed-critic and fixed-round baselines and count spending on unsolved tasks. Reporting a cost-success frontier would show whether a cheaper setting simply sacrifices correctness or produces a real efficiency advantage.

I would not route solely on the critic's uncalibrated self-confidence. Calibration, execution evidence and task-specific uncertainty would need validation on held-out problems. These are policy ideas motivated by A-ProS's cost and confidence findings, not benefits already demonstrated by the published workflow.

questions.question: What happens when judge feedback is sparse?
questions.answer: A verdict-only signal can say a candidate failed without explaining why. I would compare verdict-only, examples and richer diagnostics to quantify feedback requirements.
detail: A bare verdict can tell the system that a candidate failed without identifying the failing behavior. That makes diagnosis harder: Wrong Answer alone may correspond to an incorrect algorithm, a missed edge case or a formatting issue. Rich-feedback performance should not be assumed to survive unchanged.

I would compare verdict-only feedback, public-example diagnostics and richer accessible execution evidence on the same tasks. I would keep hidden scoring tests inaccessible and allow a separately budgeted visible reproduction step. That would measure how much the workflow depends on evidence supplied by the environment.

If richer feedback helps substantially, the contribution is partly about obtaining and validating that feedback. If verdict-only revision performs similarly, the workflow may be simpler to deploy. Either result would clarify the requirements. I would report feedback access as an experimental condition rather than treating every judge interaction as equally informative.

questions.question: What is XLAgent in 30 seconds?
questions.answer: It studies and attempts to repair bugs caused by interactions across Java-TypeScript and Python-Go boundaries, using a navigation graph, localization, contract reasoning and editing in an isolated harness.
detail: XLAgent studies defects whose repair requires coordinated changes across interacting languages. We examine Java-TypeScript and Python-Go systems, build a corpus of real fixes and test a workflow combining source navigation, localization, contract evidence, editing and execution checks. The manuscript is under review.

We mined 145 repositories, confirmed 86 broadly identified fixes and retained 31 under strict interaction criteria. The graph connected 11 of 12 fixes at boundary types it models, but did not improve localization over shell search. On five executable bugs, XLAgent more often edited both developer-file sides without establishing better repair correctness.

I carried out the project with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI. The most important lesson was that a stronger-looking representation or patch is not sufficient evidence of a repaired interaction. Leakage, incomplete issue statements and unsuitable hidden tests can change what an apparent success or failure means.
questions.caution: The manuscript is under review, and repair superiority was not established.
followups: What qualifies as a cross-language bug?

questions.question: What is the purpose of XLAgent?
questions.answer: To understand cross-language defects, recover their relationships and test whether that evidence helps an agent localize and repair both sides reliably.
detail: The purpose is to understand what breaks at a language boundary and what evidence an agent needs to repair it. A repository containing two languages is not enough; the relevant defect depends on their interaction. That leads to questions about contracts, navigation, diagnosis and evaluation.

The empirical study characterizes strict cross-language fixes. The graph attempts to recover the relationships connecting their code. The agent experiment tests whether that information changes localization and repair. Separating these parts matters: accurate edges do not automatically mean the agent uses them effectively or repairs the behavior.

The graph has useful in-scope coverage, but shell search is already strong on the tested localization tasks. Repair remains difficult and the oracle is limited. I see the contribution as an evidence-based account of those obstacles, not a claim that cross-language repair has been solved.
questions.caution: The empirical study, graph quality and repair outcomes answer different questions.
followups: Why did you choose these language pairs?

questions.question: What is a strict cross-language bug?
questions.answer: A defect whose fix changes non-test source in both languages, with those changes needed together because of how the sides interact.
detail: A strict case must repair a defect, change non-test source code in both languages and require those changes together because of how the components interact. The dependency between the changes is the important criterion. Merely observing two languages in a pull request is not enough.

If a sender and receiver disagree about the representation of a shared field and both must change to restore the exchange, that qualifies. Adding a new endpoint and client can be a feature, while two independent bug fixes in the same PR do not become an interaction bug just because they share a commit.

It determines the construct the benchmark measures. Without it, an agent could appear to solve cross-language tasks by repairing only one language's source while the other side changes only in tests or cosmetically. Applying the strict rule reduced the original 86 confirmed cases to 31 defensible interaction fixes.
questions.caution: Multiple changed languages do not automatically establish a cross-language defect.
followups: Give a positive and a negative example.

questions.question: How did you build the corpus?
questions.answer: Mine 145 repositories, find 1,206 merged PRs changing both languages, filter to 668 candidates, confirm 86 fixes, then retain 31 under strict interaction criteria.
detail: We selected 145 repositories and found 1,206 merged pull requests changing both languages of the relevant pair. Bug-term filtering and exclusions produced 668 candidates. Review retained 86 broadly confirmed fixes, and a later strict interaction review retained 31. Each stage answers a different selection question.

The early candidates received direct author review. A model proposed labels for later candidates and positive proposals were reviewed. Independent LLM judges then evaluated sampled and confirmed cases, exposing disagreement about whether both language changes were genuinely necessary. That prompted the strict reassessment.

The retained fraction is not the prevalence of cross-language bugs. Keyword filters, selection criteria and unreviewed negative predictions can miss valid cases. I present the funnel as the provenance of this corpus and preserve the exclusions, rather than interpreting 31 divided by the mined PR total as an ecosystem defect rate.
questions.caution: This pipeline is not a population prevalence estimate.
followups: What could the filters miss?

questions.question: Why did the corpus shrink from 86 to 31?
questions.answer: Stricter review required non-test changes in both languages and evidence that their interaction made both changes necessary. Many broad candidates failed that test.
detail: The original set included fixes where both languages changed but the interaction did not require both source changes. The strict review required non-test modifications on both sides and a causal dependency between them. Cases involving independent repairs, cosmetic changes, one-language source changes or non-defect work were excluded.

The resulting 31-fix set better matches the claim of coordinated cross-language repair. It also changes the taxonomy, graph coverage and executable population, so those analyses must be recomputed rather than retaining favorable numbers from the broader set. The current repair set has five strict executable bugs.

Shrinking the corpus was a correction to construct validity, not a result to hide. A smaller well-defined population is more useful than a larger collection that mixes different tasks. I now state the strict denominator explicitly and separate it from older exploratory counts when discussing the manuscript.

followups: Did the new definition change the conclusions?

questions.question: Why select Java-TypeScript and Python-Go?
questions.answer: They cover common backend/frontend or mobile-bridge patterns and infrastructure/ML client-service patterns, while exposing different interface mechanisms.
detail: Java-TypeScript is relevant to backend/frontend and mobile bridge systems, while Python-Go appears in infrastructure and machine-learning client/service software. They offer concrete but different interaction patterns, allowing us to test whether one navigation approach covers more than a single interface family.

The Java-TypeScript strict cases contain many native bridges, while Python-Go includes REST, gRPC and shared-file boundaries. That distribution matters because the graph models some string- and schema-mediated relationships much better than native bridges. A language label alone does not explain tool coverage.

These are purposively selected pairs, not a representative sample of all multilingual software. I would not generalize their category frequencies to Python-Java, C++ or private enterprise repositories without another study. The useful comparison is how the boundary mechanism interacts with the method, not a universal ranking of language-pair difficulty.
questions.caution: They are a purposive sample, not representative of every language combination.
followups: Why not Python-Java or C++?

questions.question: What repository filters did you use?
questions.answer: The mining used activity, age, stars, CI and license criteria, excluded forks and non-project examples, and required meaningful bytes from both languages.
detail: The repository search used minimum activity, age, stars, CI and license criteria and excluded forks, archived projects, tutorials, templates and demos. The paper records at least 500 stars, a push within the preceding 90 days and an age of six months. Each language also had to contribute a meaningful amount of code.

The Python-Go second-language threshold was smaller because a Go-centered infrastructure project can expose a relatively small but important Python SDK. Requiring an identical byte share would exclude some genuine interacting systems. The thresholds were therefore a tractability and relevance choice, not a claim of representative sampling.

The study favors established, public and actively maintained projects. It can miss small projects, private systems and less active repositories. I would test robustness by varying thresholds and auditing excluded groups, rather than treating the selected corpus as the whole multilingual ecosystem.
questions.caution: The resulting corpus excludes much private and small-project software.
followups: How would you test robustness to those filters?

questions.question: What is the largest strict root-cause category?
questions.answer: Contract and schema mismatches: 11 of 31 strict fixes, about 35%.
detail: Contract and schema mismatches are the largest strict root-cause category: 11 of 31 fixes, approximately 35%. These are cases where interacting components disagree about an interface assumption, such as a route, field, enum value or message shape.

A schema mismatch explains why the exchange is wrong. REST or gRPC describes how the components communicate. The same conceptual root cause can occur through different boundaries, so I keep those labels separate rather than treating every gRPC defect as one kind of bug.

The result suggests that explicit contract evidence is worth investigating, but the count does not prove our contract-reasoning component improves repairs. That requires an intervention study, whose current result is inconclusive. I use 11 of 31 for the strict set, not the superseded 27-of-86 count from the broader corpus.
questions.caution: Do not use the older 27-of-86 count for the strict set.
followups: How is that different from a boundary category?

questions.question: Which boundaries dominate?
questions.answer: Native bridges account for 13 strict fixes, REST 6, gRPC 4, shared files 2, subprocesses 2 and other boundaries 4.
detail: The strict set has 13 native-bridge fixes, 6 REST fixes, 4 gRPC fixes, 2 shared-file fixes, 2 subprocess fixes and 4 other cases. Native bridges are therefore the largest single boundary group, while service and shared-data boundaries also make up a substantial portion.

All native-bridge and subprocess cases in this corpus are Java-TypeScript. The gRPC and shared-file cases are Python-Go. That helps explain why the same graph has strong coverage on one pair and weak coverage on the other: the supported boundary mechanisms differ.

A tool advertised as cross-language should be evaluated by the exchanges it actually models. Supporting several parsers is not enough if the important runtime bridge is missing. These counts describe our selected corpus and are not estimates of how often each boundary fails across all real software.
questions.caution: These are corpus counts, not ecosystem frequencies.
followups: Why does graph coverage differ between pairs?

questions.question: How reliable are the labels?
questions.answer: Inclusion required substantial interpretation. Judges agreed more on whether both languages changed than on whether the changes depended on each other.
detail: It was easier for raters to determine whether source in both languages changed than to determine whether the changes depended on each other. In the full confirmed-fix review, the reported kappa is 0.97 for two-language non-test changes but 0.34 for interdependence. The second judgment requires substantially more interpretation.

The strict inclusion review used recorded rationales and excluded uncertain cases under its stated decision rule. The author also reviewed the cases. That provides a more transparent basis for the 31-fix corpus than accepting every model-proposed positive label.

Agreement is not ground truth, especially when LLM judges can share assumptions and training biases. I would strengthen this with independently blinded expert review and adjudication of disagreements. The current labels are a documented operationalization of the construct, and the disagreement is itself evidence about how difficult that construct is to apply.
questions.caution: Agreement is not ground truth, and LLM judges can share biases.
followups: How would you add independent expert review?

questions.question: Can 31 divided by 1206 estimate prevalence?
questions.answer: No. The pipeline uses keyword filtering, selective review and unreviewed model-negative candidates. The retained fraction reflects this process, not all cross-language bugs in an ecosystem.
detail: The 31 strict fixes come from a filtered pipeline, not a random sample of every relevant repair. Keyword matching, repository criteria, classifier decisions and selective review all affect which tasks can reach the final set. The denominator of 1,206 is therefore not an unbiased opportunity population for estimating prevalence.

A genuine interaction bug might lack the selected bug terms or be rejected by the model and never manually reexamined. Conversely, changing two languages is only a coarse candidate criterion. The strict confirmation process improves label precision among retained cases but does not recover every missed positive.

I would sample merged PRs independently of those filters, manually inspect a representative subset and estimate inclusion probability with uncertainty. I would also audit model negatives. Until then, I report the selection funnel and category frequencies within the confirmed strict corpus, not a general percentage of all defects.
questions.caution: Do not interpret the confirmation ratio as a general defect rate.
followups: How would you estimate missed positives?

questions.question: What was the false-negative concern in mining?
questions.answer: The model's negative labels were not all manually checked, so relevant fixes may have been missed before the strict review.
detail: Reviewing model-positive labels can remove false positives, but it does not reveal valid cases hidden among model-negative predictions. Some of the later negative labels were not all manually reviewed, so the corpus can have incomplete recall even when retained cases receive careful confirmation.

I would draw a random stratified sample of rejected candidates, apply the strict criteria blindly and measure how often true cases were missed. The paper also reports a later model check against the first manually reviewed candidates, but that does not eliminate uncertainty about the entire rejected population.

This is why I avoid prevalence estimates and claims of complete coverage. The corpus is a useful documented set of interaction fixes. To make it a measurement of how common such fixes are, we would need a sampling design and false-negative audit that support that stronger inference.
questions.caution: Reviewing every positive removes some false positives, not false negatives.

questions.question: Give a concrete cross-language example.
questions.answer: In the kagent motivating case, model options cross from a Go-side service into a Python client. Fixing only representation on one side can leave the other side interpreting them incorrectly.
detail: In the motivating repair case, model options travel from a Go-side service to a Python client. The interaction depends on both the representation sent across the boundary and the receiving API's expectations. A patch that changes only one representation can still leave the complete path wrong.

Hidden tests for the resolved case check the Go side. The patch assessment found XLAgent candidates that passed that check while mishandling the Python-side options, for example leaving values in an inappropriate representation or field. That makes the case useful for explaining false success about end-to-end repair.

I would construct a visible behavioral reproduction spanning the producer and consumer, assert the transmitted type and value and verify the final client behavior. The lesson is not simply that both files must change. It is that the contract joining them must work, which requires evidence beyond a one-sided test pass.
questions.caution: Use the manuscript's actual case; invented endpoint names would only be an illustration.
followups: Why can the hidden tests miss the other side?
