questions.question: What is the cross-language graph?
questions.answer: It combines per-language symbols and references from SCIP with explicit edges across REST, headers, payloads, enums, signals and protobuf-mediated RPCs.
detail: The graph begins with per-language symbols and references from SCIP. We add explicit cross-language relationships for supported routes, headers, payloads, enums, signals and protobuf services. A boundary edge records the mediator connecting two sites, making the relation inspectable rather than an unexplained similarity link.

SCIP does not always provide the containing body for references, so tree-sitter supplies source ranges and supports extraction rules. The agent can then ask about a symbol's boundary or contract through compact path-and-line outputs instead of reading the complete graph representation.

This is a navigation and dependency graph, not a sound complete call graph for all runtime behavior. Dynamic dispatch, constructed names and unsupported native bridges can be missed. Its value needs two evaluations: whether the recovered edges are correct and whether using them improves an agent outcome. XLAgent found those are separate questions.

followups: How are routes matched?

questions.question: What is SCIP used for?
questions.answer: SCIP provides structured symbols and references inside each language, giving stable entities that cross-language edges can connect.
detail: SCIP supplies structured symbol definitions and references within a language. Those stable entities give the graph endpoints that cross-language edges can connect. Instead of linking arbitrary text fragments, a relation can identify a particular client site, handler, type or RPC symbol.

We add containing function-body ranges using tree-sitter where the index lacks them. References can then be attributed to call, type-use or related edges. For Java projects that cannot be built by the semantic indexer, the system can fall back to definitions-only syntax extraction.

The fallback preserves some navigation but loses semantic reference information. I would not describe all snapshots as equally complete because they share the same output schema. Indexing success, fallback use and boundary coverage need to be reported separately so a user understands what the graph can and cannot justify.

questions.question: Why use tree-sitter too?

detail: Tree-sitter gives syntax trees and source ranges even when full semantic indexing is incomplete. We use it to recover definition bodies and extract recognizable interface patterns. This lets the graph associate references with containing code and inspect routes or payload declarations structurally.

A parser can recognize a client call containing a literal route or a constructed URL expression. Additional rules still have to determine the method, normalized path and matching handler. The syntax tree is evidence for those rules, not an automatic proof of the runtime connection.

Parsing does not resolve every dynamic receiver, configuration branch or reflection mechanism. I therefore combine it with semantic symbols and mark heuristic cases rather than presenting an AST as complete program understanding. In the study, the final question remains empirical: how much useful structure is recovered and whether the agent benefits from it.

questions.question: How do you connect REST clients and handlers?
questions.answer: Extract HTTP methods and normalized route templates, fold supported constant URL expressions, then match clients to handlers through the mediator.
detail: We extract client calls and server route registrations, normalize the HTTP method and path and match their route templates. A small constant evaluator handles supported concatenations, f-strings, template literals and formatted URL expressions. Resolved endpoints are connected through the route mediator.

The output can show the actual client and handler symbols and the path that justifies the match. Guards and payload information can then expose a possible inconsistency, such as a client calling an endpoint that is registered only conditionally. A possible inconsistency still needs diagnosis rather than automatic repair.

Reverse proxies, dynamic registration and configuration-dependent prefixes can make textual route matching incomplete or wrong. I would retain unresolved cases and assess precision by edge kind. The paper's coverage is strongest on the modeled string-mediated boundaries, so I do not generalize that performance to arbitrary dynamic web architectures.
questions.caution: Dynamic routing, proxies and conditional configuration can defeat static matching.
followups: How would you handle a reverse proxy?

questions.question: How do gRPC edges work?
questions.answer: Proto definitions become a shared indexed mediator, linking a client stub call to the RPC method and then to its server implementation.
detail: For gRPC, the protobuf service definition provides an explicit cross-language agreement. The system indexes proto definitions and links a client stub call to the corresponding RPC method and that method to its server implementation. This creates a path through a shared schema rather than relying only on similar function names.

The service and message definitions constrain the relation more strongly than an arbitrary header assembled in a dictionary. In the labeled sample, gRPC edges were particularly precise and make up a large share of the cross-language edge population.

Correct recovered RPC edges do not show that every RPC was found or that every runtime behavior is covered. Generated code, wrappers and indexing scope still matter. I therefore separate estimated edge precision, graph coverage of reference fixes and actual localization benefit; a strong result on the first measure did not establish a gain on the last.
questions.caution: Strong sampled precision does not establish complete recall.
followups: Why can gRPC be easier than HTTP headers?

questions.question: How big is the graph?
questions.answer: The draft reports 9,605 boundary edges across the indexed snapshots, including 8,565 cross-language edges and 1,040 same-language REST route edges.

questions.question: What does the 91% precision estimate mean?
questions.answer: A stratified labeled sample estimates that 91.1% of the 8,565 cross-language edges are directly correct, or 94.3% if indirect links count.
detail: The 91.1% strict estimate concerns directly correct edges among 8,565 cross-language edges, weighted by the sizes of the sampled strata. Counting indirect but relevant links yields 94.3%. The strict reported uncertainty interval is broad, approximately 77% through 93%.

The edge kinds have different population sizes and precision. gRPC dominates the corpus and was highly accurate in the sample, while headers are harder. Taking an unweighted sample fraction could misrepresent the true mix. The estimate therefore combines labeled outcomes with the actual stratum sizes.

This is not a manual verification of every edge, a recall estimate or a guarantee about the same-language REST edges. It also relies partly on LLM judgments, with author review as an additional perspective. I state the population and uncertainty alongside the rounded 91% headline so its scope stays clear.
questions.caution: This is estimated precision, not recall, and excludes same-language route edges.
followups: Why not use raw sample accuracy?

questions.question: What graph coverage did you obtain?
questions.answer: It connected both halves for 11 of 12 strict fixes at the modeled REST, gRPC and shared-file boundaries. Across all indexed strict fixes it connected 13 of 30.
detail: The graph connects both halves of 11 of the 12 strict fixes involving the boundary kinds it models: REST, gRPC and shared files. That is a strong result for those modeled relationships, but it is not coverage of all 31 strict fixes.

Across the strict cases with both sides indexed, it connects 13 of 30. Native bridges and subprocess boundaries account for much of the gap. The difference is useful because it shows where the representation stops rather than allowing a favorable in-scope percentage to hide unsupported mechanisms.

Coverage is assessed relative to code changed by the developer fix, and indexing itself is gold-guided. It therefore does not directly measure end-to-end discovery on an unseen deployment issue. I use the result to characterize the representation and then test localization independently; that experiment found no measurable graph benefit on the chosen tasks.

questions.question: What is a graph-connected bug?
questions.answer: Within the stated hop limit, graph entities in developer-changed files on each side are linked through a boundary edge, shared schema or common boundary.
detail: A bug is graph-connected when the reference fix's code on each language side is related through a boundary edge within the defined hop limit, including the allowed shared-schema and common-boundary cases. The criterion asks whether the graph contains a relevant connection between the known fix locations.

It separates a representation failure from an agent-use failure. If the graph never relates the implicated sites, expecting it to guide the localizer is unrealistic. If it does connect them but the localizer still gains nothing, the issue is different, such as redundant lexical evidence or poor tool use.

It is not proof that an agent can discover a novel defect or that a patch following the edge is correct. The developer fix supplies evaluation locations, and the graph construction uses the fix-guided scope. Those are important conditions behind the coverage result and must be disclosed when discussing deployment relevance.
questions.caution: Gold-guided coverage should not be presented as deployment-time end-to-end recall.
followups: How does indexing use the reference fix?

questions.question: Was graph construction gold-guided?
questions.answer: Yes. Modules containing developer-changed non-test files were chosen for indexing, which uses information unavailable for a new unseen issue.
detail: Yes. We selected modules containing non-test files changed in the developer fix for indexing. An agent facing a new issue would not know those files in advance. The decision made the representation experiment tractable, but it introduces privileged information about where relevant code may be located.

The resulting graph quality and coverage should be read as measurements under that scoped setup, not as the full cost and recall of deployment-time indexing. Even though graph-enabled localizers did not improve on shell search, the gold-guided choice remains a limitation rather than disappearing because the result is null.

I would choose the indexing scope independently of the fix, such as the entire repository or a budgeted issue-driven module selection policy. I would measure indexing time, missing dependencies and agent outcomes jointly. That would test whether the structure can be obtained and used without reference-answer knowledge.
questions.caution: This is an important limitation even though the graph did not improve localization.
followups: What would a fair deployment simulation change?

questions.question: What is the agent pipeline?
questions.answer: A read-only localizer finds relevant sites; contract reasoning summarizes boundary evidence; an editor patches; a validation gate checks new basic errors; visible tests can trigger another round.
detail: The agent starts with an issue statement and an isolated pre-fix snapshot. A read-only localizer produces structured locations and boundary evidence. The system groups relevant graph edges into contracts, applies deterministic checks and obtains up to three model-generated fix hypotheses where a contract is involved.

An editor uses the report and evidence to patch the repository. A gate checks new syntax, compile and lint problems. Visible repository tests compare patched behavior with the original snapshot, and new failures can trigger another investigation and editing round.

Hidden fail-to-pass tests are used for scoring outside the agent loop. That separation prevents evaluation answers from becoming feedback. The architecture makes the process inspectable, but each component's benefit is an empirical question. The current ablations do not establish a measurable repair contribution for any individual component.
questions.caution: A diagram describes implementation, not evidence that each component improves outcomes.
followups: What does the gate guarantee?

questions.question: Why separate localization from editing?
questions.answer: It creates an explicit read-only evidence-gathering phase and a structured handoff before modifications, which makes the process easier to inspect.
detail: A separate read-only localization phase makes the evidence-gathering decision explicit before code changes. It produces a structured handoff naming locations, roles and boundary relationships. That helps us inspect whether a later patch followed a plausible diagnosis and whether both interaction partners were considered.

Inspectability is not the same as a performance advantage. To ask whether the split helps, we compare it with a matched single agent using comparable machinery and a combined step budget, in addition to the stock baseline. That addresses a narrower causal question than a broad baseline comparison.

The matched single agent comes close on the five repair tasks, and component removals preserve much of the two-sided-edit pattern. I therefore cannot attribute that pattern to the role split alone. I defend the architecture as a tested hypothesis and an auditable implementation, while keeping the causal claim limited.
questions.caution: The current five-bug evidence cannot attribute two-sided edits to the split alone.
followups: Did the ablation establish a benefit?

questions.question: What does contract reasoning do?
questions.answer: Group edges by route, header, RPC or payload, check deterministic mismatches and ask a model for up to three fix hypotheses grounded in those contracts.
detail: The system groups boundary edges by their mediator, such as a route, RPC, header or shared payload. Deterministic checks look for mismatches including fields or enum members present on one side, unmatched routes or an RPC with callers but no detected server.

A model uses those contracts and findings to propose up to three fix hypotheses. This is intended to turn a collection of relationships into an explanation of how the exchange may be broken. If no relevant contract is found, the step is skipped rather than manufacturing one.

A one-sided field can be legitimate, and a graph omission can look like a missing handler. The editor must verify the hypothesis against the actual code and behavior. In the current evaluation, removing the contract component did not measurably change repairs. The design is therefore not evidence that every contract warning is a bug or that the reasoning step improves correctness.
questions.caution: A flagged difference is not automatically a bug; legitimate asymmetry exists.
followups: How would you measure hypothesis grounding?

questions.question: What does the validation gate check?
questions.answer: Syntax, compilation and selected lint or vet checks on touched code, comparing against the unpatched snapshot so pre-existing errors are not blamed on the patch.
detail: The gate runs checks appropriate to touched code, including syntax, compilation and selected lint or vet tools. For Python that includes compilation and pyflakes; for touched Go packages it includes formatting, build and vet checks. It compares against the original snapshot so existing failures are not automatically blamed on the patch.

If a dependency prevents a check from running, the system records a skip rather than claiming a pass. If localization identified both sides but the first patch leaves one side unchanged, it can return a warning for reconsideration; a later deliberate one-sided submission remains possible.

It catches some newly introduced basic failures under runnable checks. It does not certify semantics, end-to-end behavior or that all required changes were made. I keep gate acceptance separate from visible test outcomes, hidden scoring and patch correctness assessment because each provides different evidence.
questions.caution: Passing the gate does not prove semantic correctness; a deliberate one-sided patch can still be submitted.
followups: Why compare with the original snapshot?

questions.question: How is feedback routed?
questions.answer: Visible repository tests run after gate acceptance. New failures on one side send investigation to that side; failures on both sides direct attention toward the interaction contract.
detail: After a patch passes the gate, visible repository tests run for the changed code. Their results are compared with the unpatched snapshot to identify new failures. A failure on one side sends investigation toward that side; failures on both sides direct attention to the shared contract.

A test can already fail because of the old environment or unrelated code. Treating every observed failure as a regression would send the agent toward the wrong explanation. The baseline comparison helps attribute newly introduced problems, although it still depends on a valid and sufficiently informative test environment.

The hidden scoring tests do not drive this feedback loop. They evaluate the final candidate afterward. The routing itself is a heuristic, and the ablation did not establish a measurable repair benefit on the five tasks. I therefore describe how it works without claiming that the mechanism was proven effective.

questions.question: Did the graph improve localization?
questions.answer: No measurable improvement was found. On 12 strict localization bugs, the shell-only localizer found both developer-file sides in every run.
detail: No measurable improvement was found. On the strict 12-bug localization set, the shell-only condition found developer-changed files on both sides in every run. The mean file-level counts were 10.7 for full XL navigation, 11.7 for graph navigation without boundary edges and 12.0 for shell.

Many of these relationships are mediated by a shared name, such as a route fragment, type or configuration discriminator. Searching the name in both languages can reveal the same endpoints as the graph. The representation may be accurate without adding information the localizer lacks.

The experiment does not prove graphs are useless for all interaction defects. It shows no benefit on this task distribution and setup, which also includes gold-guided indexing. I would next stratify cases by lexical overlap and indirection instead of increasing graph complexity without a specific hypothesis.
questions.caution: A useful graph representation is not the same as a useful intervention for this agent.
followups: Why might the benchmark hide a graph benefit?

questions.question: Why could grep perform as well as the graph?
questions.answer: Many boundaries are mediated by a shared route, type, enum or configuration string. Searching that name across languages can reveal the same endpoints.
detail: The graph often matches endpoints through a string shared across languages. If the issue or a discovered site exposes that same route, enum or type name, a shell search can locate both sides directly. The graph then organizes a relation the agent can already recover cheaply.

The shell condition searched across language files for shared identifiers. The full localizer also used graph tools, so the null result is not explained only by never invoking them. The more relevant explanation is that the additional structure was often redundant for finding these locations.

I would distinguish name-aligned cases from those involving wrappers, renamed concepts or nonlocal semantic dependencies. A graph might be more useful in the latter group, but that is a hypothesis to test on independently selected tasks. The existing result limits a broad graph-benefit claim rather than establishing universal equivalence.

questions.question: How many executable repair bugs were there?

I would report the five-task scope explicitly and expand executable coverage before making a general claim about multilingual repair.

questions.question: What are the main repair results?
questions.answer: XLAgent edited developer-changed files in both languages on an average 4.0 of 5 bugs, versus 2.7 for baseline and 3.0 for the matched single agent.
detail: XLAgent edits developer-changed files in both languages on an average 4.0 of the five bugs, compared with 2.7 for the stock baseline and 3.0 for the matched single agent. These are averages across three replicates, and the metric describes reference-file overlap on both sides.

questions.question: What is the difference between two-sided and correct?
questions.answer: Two-sided means the patch touches a counted source file in each language. Correctness requires the intended behavior to work, including the contract connecting those sides.
detail: A two-sided patch changes counted source files in both languages. In the strict metric, each side includes a file also changed by the developer fix. Correctness instead asks whether the intended interaction behaves properly without introducing regressions. Those are different properties.

An agent can touch both relevant files but implement the wrong contract. Conversely, a valid alternative may repair the behavior through different files or a justified one-sided change. Reference overlap is therefore a diagnostic proxy for where the agent looked, not a complete oracle for what it accomplished.

I report patch shape alongside hidden test resolution and independent side-specific assessment. If the measures disagree, I investigate rather than replacing the harder outcome with the favorable proxy. For future work I would make cross-boundary behavioral tests the primary endpoint and use file overlap only to explain the process.
questions.caution: The metric describes patch shape and reference overlap, not complete behavior.
followups: Can a valid repair be one-sided?

questions.question: What is cross-language blindness?
questions.answer: In this paper it means changing non-test code in only one language, despite a strict task whose reference fix changes both sides.
detail: In this paper, a cross-language-blind patch changes non-test code in only one of the counted languages. It signals that the agent may have ignored the interaction partner on a task whose reference repair requires both sides. The name describes an observed patch property, not a psychological claim about the model.

If an issue involves a sender and receiver, changing only the sender is worth inspecting. The localization report and the gate can prompt the editor to reconsider an untouched side. This makes a common failure pattern observable and offers evidence for trajectory analysis.

A developer’s patch is not the only possible implementation. A valid repair might resolve the mismatch entirely at one boundary endpoint. questions.question: Why are hidden tests not definitive here?
questions.answer: They exercise one language, so passing can miss a defect on the other side. Three suites also depend on developer-introduced names and can reject alternate valid repairs.
detail: Each hidden fail-to-pass suite exercises one language. A candidate can therefore satisfy the scored side while leaving the other side's contract handling wrong. The kagent assessment provides that kind of disagreement: some resolved full-system patches are not judged correct on both sides.

Three of the five suites also depend on names or fixtures introduced by the developer's implementation. An alternative repair can implement the intended behavior under different internals and fail the overlaid suite. Passing and failing therefore both need more careful interpretation than the raw verdict suggests.

These limitations do not excuse every agent failure. I would inspect independent behavior on both endpoints, validate the environment and compare the candidate with the actual requirement. The current results establish that one-sided hidden resolution is an incomplete measure of cross-language correctness, not that the proposed system secretly repairs all rejected cases.

questions.question: What is implementation-coupled testing?
questions.answer: A test assumes an internal helper, private member or new identifier used by the reference patch, even when the user-visible requirement allows other implementations.
detail: Implementation coupling occurs when a test requires details of the reference repair rather than only the intended behavior. Examples include a newly named helper, a private field or an internal fixture structure. A semantically valid alternative can then fail even though it honors the user-visible contract.

Three of the five strict repair suites have this concern. Some overlaid tests call names that exist only after the developer's chosen fix, while others mock private members. If the agent uses another internal design, the test may not compile or may reject it before checking the real interaction.

I would derive tests from externally justified requirements and execute the producer-consumer path without depending on reference-only internals. Specified public API names can legitimately matter, so not every naming requirement is invalid coupling. The classification needs evidence that the test demands an unstated implementation choice.

questions.question: Did the judges validate repair superiority?
questions.answer: No. The LLM judges counted 3 of 15 XLAgent patches fully correct versus 4 baseline patches; the author pass was stricter, finding 0 versus 1.
detail: No. The LLM judges counted 3 of 15 full-system patches as correct on all sides and 4 of 15 baseline patches. The author's stricter pass found 0 and 1 respectively. Neither assessment supports a correctness advantage for XLAgent over the baseline.

Model judges can agree with each other while using a permissive interpretation of partial behavior. The author disagreed substantially with their patch labels. Reporting only the more favorable assessment would hide a central uncertainty about how correctness was measured.

The useful finding is not a superiority claim but the need for a stronger behavioral oracle and a clearer assessment rubric. I would add blinded expert review and interaction-level tests, while retaining the existing labels and their disagreement. Judge consensus is evidence about a review process, not a replacement for validated end-to-end correctness.
questions.caution: Judge consensus is an imperfect measurement, not ground truth.

questions.question: What did the ablations show?
questions.answer: Removing boundary edges, contracts, feedback or navigation did not measurably change repairs, and two-sided edits persisted across conditions.
detail: The ablations remove boundary edges, contract reasoning, feedback or navigation tools, with a matched single-agent condition added to the stock baseline. They run on the same strict executable bugs in the same contemporaneous batch, so the comparison avoids mixing backend versions.

Two-sided edits persist across the component removals, and no single component measurably changes repairs on the five tasks. Resolution changes only on the one bug resolved by any condition. The matched single agent also comes close on the patch-shape measure.

I cannot attribute the pattern to one graph component or to splitting localization and editing alone. I also cannot conclude all components are equivalent everywhere, because the task set is tiny and the oracles are limited. The next experiment needs more independent tasks chosen to discriminate the hypothesized mechanisms, not more confident language about the same outcomes.
questions.caution: Null evidence here is not proof of equal performance in all settings.
followups: What larger controlled experiment is needed?

questions.question: Why add a matched single agent?
questions.answer: A stock baseline differs in several ways. The matched control keeps more of the workflow machinery and budget while combining localization and editing in one agent.
detail: The full system and a stock agent differ in prompts, tools, gate behavior, feedback and organization. If their outcomes differ, that broad comparison cannot identify whether the cause is two agents, additional resources or some other shared intervention. A practical baseline and a causal control serve different purposes.

The matched single agent localizes and edits without a separate localizer, using a combined step budget and much of the surrounding evaluation machinery. It tests the role split more directly than the stock baseline does. The comparison still has residual differences related to the localization report and associated checks.

Its two-sided developer-file count is 3.0 of five, compared with 4.0 for the full system, but per-bug evidence is too limited to isolate a cause. I therefore describe the split as a plausible design choice whose independent performance contribution is not established by this experiment.

questions.question: Why not report a significance win on five bugs?
questions.answer: A five-task paired sign test has very low resolution: even all five favoring one system gives a minimum two-sided p-value of 0.0625.
detail: With five independent paired tasks, even all five favoring one condition gives a smallest attainable two-sided sign-test p-value of 0.0625. The experiment cannot produce a conventional 0.05 significance result under that test, regardless of how favorable the task-level pattern looks.

Three runs per bug help describe stochastic variation on that bug. They do not create fifteen independent bug problems. Treating every patch as a separate task would underestimate dependence and overstate how much evidence we have about the broader population.

The manuscript uses per-bug outcomes and replicate ranges for repair rather than a significance-win headline. I would expand the number and diversity of independent tasks and predefine a practically meaningful endpoint. The present data can expose mechanisms and limitations, but it cannot establish broad statistical repair superiority.

questions.question: Why rerun all repair conditions in one batch?
questions.answer: The provider's model behind an alias changed during earlier experiments. A single contemporaneous batch with the same fingerprint reduces version drift as a confound.
detail: The provider changed the model served behind a requested alias during earlier experiments. The same request name therefore did not guarantee the same underlying system. Comparing conditions run on different backend versions could attribute a model change to a workflow intervention.

We reran the strict repair and ablation conditions in a single contemporaneous batch on one reported backend version. The 105 runs had a consistent response fingerprint, and the protocol would stop on a changed fingerprint. That makes the current comparison cleaner than pooling the earlier mixed batches.

A stable fingerprint is useful evidence, not complete access to the provider's implementation. Stochastic outputs and task dependence still remain. I preserve returned identities, timestamps and trajectories so others can audit the comparison, and I distinguish reproducing the recorded analysis from regenerating identical future API outputs.
questions.caution: This controls one source of variation, not all stochastic or temporal effects.

questions.question: What are the limits of the issue statements?
questions.answer: The strict localization set uses linked-issue material; 19 of 31 corpus statements otherwise came from PR descriptions that can disclose the fix. Repair tasks use short PR titles without linked issues.
detail: Nineteen of the 31 strict corpus cases otherwise rely on PR descriptions, which often reveal the fix. The strict localization set uses linked-issue material to reduce that exposure. The five repair cases have no linked issue and use short PR titles as their statements.

Including a solution-bearing PR description can leak the answer. Removing it can leave a title that omits required behavior or context. A title-only task can therefore be both less leaky and less well specified. Those are separate properties, and improving one does not automatically solve the other.

I would collect contemporaneous issue reports and preserve what a developer knew before the fix. Independent reviewers should check whether the report defines the intended behavior without requiring reference-patch knowledge. Until that is available, I treat statement quality as a limitation affecting what an unresolved or apparently correct patch means.

questions.question: What leakage did you discover?
questions.answer: Before isolation, agents could read developer fixes through Git history, local caches or network access. The record reports this in 13 of 16 baseline runs.
detail: Before isolation, 13 of 16 baseline runs accessed developer fixes or later solution-bearing information through sources such as Git history, local caches or the network. This was direct runtime access during evaluation, not an inference about what the model might have memorized in pretraining.

A later audit found that graph-tool checkouts held uncommitted fixed source. Eight runs were exposed through that channel and had to be replaced. The agent's own workspace could look clean while a tool server still returned post-fix evidence.

Those observations invalidated affected runs as evidence of independent repair. We added isolation, tool-output auditing and reruns. The general lesson is that evaluation includes every evidence surface reachable through a tool, not just the prompt or main checkout. An apparent benchmark success can be a retrieval of the answer rather than a repair capability.
questions.caution: This is runtime solution leakage, separate from possible pretraining contamination.
followups: What safeguards did you implement?

questions.question: How did you prevent runtime leakage?
questions.answer: Run each agent on a single-commit pre-fix snapshot with no remote, deny network and outside-file access, isolate scoring artifacts and audit trajectories and tool outputs.
detail: Each run uses its own pre-fix snapshot with a single commit and no remote. The sandbox denies network access and access outside the run directory and permitted build caches. Hidden scoring artifacts remain inaccessible to the solving agent. Removing a remote alone would not block local history, caches or other file channels.

Before paid evaluation, reference-policy and escape-attempt checks exercise the harness. We audit trajectories and tool outputs for access to later fixes, scoring material and outside information. Graph-tool checkouts also need snapshot and cleanliness checks because they can supply information indirectly.

The retained runs passed the defined audit after exposed runs were replaced. That is stronger evidence than trusting an instruction not to inspect the answer, but it is not a formal proof of perfect isolation. I report the boundary and known audit coverage so the claim remains testable.

questions.question: What is an oracle-policy sanity test?
questions.answer: A scripted reference-fix policy exercises the sandbox, gate, feedback and scorer to check that the environment can recognize the known fix before agent evaluation.
detail: An oracle-policy run applies the known developer fix through the same environment and evaluation path to check that the harness can recognize it. It exercises the sandbox, tool server, gate, feedback and scoring before interpreting agent failures. This is a diagnostic control with privileged information.

If the reference fix cannot pass because a dependency, test recipe or scorer is broken, an agent's failure does not meaningfully measure repair ability. The control helps locate that kind of infrastructure problem before spending on a large batch of model runs.

Reference success does not prove tests accept every valid alternative or check both interaction sides. That is exactly the implementation-coupling concern in the repair set. Oracle-policy runs also must never be pooled with agent performance, since they have the answer. They validate the measurement path rather than demonstrate autonomous capability.
questions.caution: Oracle policies are not agent performance results and must not be pooled with them.
followups: What if the reference fix does not pass?

questions.question: What is your strongest takeaway from XLAgent?
questions.answer: Better-looking structure and more two-sided edits are insufficient. We need an isolated, valid measurement process that can tell whether the cross-language behavior was repaired.
detail: The strongest takeaway is that useful-looking structure and promising patch shape are not enough. A graph can recover correct relationships without improving localization, and a patch can change both languages without repairing their interaction. The measurement must support the actual behavioral claim.

A one-sided test can pass while the other side remains wrong, while a reference-coupled test can reject an alternative valid implementation. Combined with runtime answer leakage, that means both apparent successes and apparent failures need careful attribution. The environment is part of the scientific argument.

That motivates behavioral reproductions, explicit contracts and isolated evaluation with matched controls. questions.question: What is a falsifiable research hypothesis for you?
questions.answer: Contract-grounded reproductions improve independently assessed cross-boundary behavior compared with equally budgeted unstructured feedback on the same bugs.

questions.question: What would you work on if graphs keep showing null effects?
questions.answer: Study where agents lack information rather than adding structure by default: ambiguous contracts, indirect boundaries, incomplete reproductions and weak evaluation oracles.
detail: My interest is reliable repair, not proving that graphs must help. If graph-enabled agents continue to match shell search, I would ask what information is missing in the actual failures. I would stratify tasks by lexical overlap and boundary mechanism to find whether there is a population where structural evidence adds information unavailable from simple search.

I would compare the simplest plausible intervention against a strong baseline and retain the null finding if it remains. Method flexibility is part of the research strategy.

questions.question: How do you choose a research question?
questions.answer: I start from a failure I can reproduce and ask what the current evidence cannot distinguish. I then try to name competing explanations and design a small experiment that separates them. That keeps the research question connected to a measurable uncertainty instead of starting from a fashionable architecture.
detail: I start from a failure I can reproduce and ask what the current evidence cannot distinguish. I then try to name competing explanations and design a small experiment that separates them. That keeps the research question connected to a measurable uncertainty instead of starting from a fashionable architecture.

In XLAgent, editing both languages and passing a hidden suite could suggest success, but the suite checked only one side. The competing explanation was that the agent satisfied the scored component while leaving the interaction wrong. Side-specific patch assessment made that distinction visible.

I prefer a question whose negative result would still teach something. If a graph adds no value because lexical search already supplies the information, that finding can redirect effort toward diagnosis or oracles. A good question should change the next decision regardless of whether the proposed method wins.

questions.question: How do you avoid overfitting a benchmark?
questions.answer: Freeze evaluation tasks and criteria, keep development cases separate, disclose model access and test use, and replicate on new repositories or later time windows.
detail: I would freeze the evaluation criteria and hold out tasks that do not guide prompt or tool design. Cases repeatedly inspected while developing the method are effectively development data, even if no model weights are trained. That information history needs to be documented.

I would replicate on different repositories or a later prospective task window and retain the same scoring protocol. The information boundary would include files, tools, history and human access to solution-bearing material, not just which JSON file contains the test IDs.

An agent can overfit through benchmark-specific scaffolding and visible hidden-test assumptions. A clean split helps only when access is actually enforced and the oracle checks the intended behavior. I would therefore pair the held-out design with isolation, provenance records and an audit of what was known when each method decision was made.

questions.question: What if the advisor disagrees with your interpretation?
questions.answer: Ask which assumption or evidence differs, reproduce the comparison together, and design a test that could distinguish the interpretations.

questions.question: How would you prioritize with limited compute?
questions.answer: Validate the harness, run a small pilot, eliminate irrelevant conditions, and spend on matched comparisons that answer the core question.
detail: I would validate the harness and known reference cases first, then run a small pilot before allocating a large model budget. Early failures in environment setup, leakage or scoring invalidate many more runs than a slightly suboptimal model choice. The cheapest useful experiment is one whose result I can interpret.

I would prioritize comparisons that distinguish the main explanations and remove conditions that do not answer the core question. I would match relevant budgets, record spend on failed tasks and decide stopping criteria in advance rather than expanding until a favorable result appears.

API cost is only part of research cost. Environment work, annotation and debugging also matter. I would invest in reusable artifacts and logs so a failed batch still informs the next decision. If a pilot shows the oracle cannot recognize independent repairs, I would fix that before buying more agent trajectories.
questions.caution: This is my proposed approach, not a claim that the experiment or design has already been implemented.
followups: What would you stop doing?

questions.question: What makes your work reproducible?
questions.answer: Reproducibility needs exact artifacts, environments, model-response records, scoring rules and a clear boundary between visible feedback and hidden evaluation.
detail: I distinguish rerunning the analysis from regenerating identical model outputs. Exact trajectories from a changing API may be impossible to recreate, but retained prompts, responses, patches and scoring artifacts can still allow another researcher to audit the original conclusions.

The package needs immutable task and snapshot IDs, environment recipes, model-response identities, configurations, visible-versus-hidden boundaries, exclusions and versioned analysis. A table cell should be traceable to the retained runs that produced it. Discarded contaminated batches should remain documented as exclusions.

I would state which artifacts are actually released and which still need preparation, rather than promising one-command reproduction before verifying it. Reproducibility is a chain of evidence and executable checks, not just a GitHub link. My project experience has made that distinction central to how I design later experiments.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: I am Md Sifat Hossain, a University of Dhaka CSE graduate and software engineer at Therap BD Ltd. My research has progressed from benchmarking LLM code generation to feedback-driven programming and cross-language debugging.
detail: I am Md Sifat Hossain. I studied Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Dhaka and now work as a software engineer at Therap BD Ltd. Alongside engineering, I have been researching LLM-based programming and the reliability of software agents.

In LLM-ProS I built evaluation infrastructure for first-attempt program generation on ICPC problems. A-ProS extended the question to iterative generation and debugging feedback, where I worked on orchestration, logging, ablations and calibration. My current XLAgent project studies cross-language interaction bugs and the limits of evaluating their repairs.

I want to pursue doctoral research on evidence-grounded diagnosis and repair. What motivates me is understanding what an automated change really establishes, rather than only producing a plausible patch. I bring practical system-building experience and a growing interest in the experimental methods needed to support reliable claims.

questions.question: What is the thread connecting all three projects?
questions.answer: They ask how to obtain reliable evidence for automated programming: measure first-attempt capability, study feedback-based improvement, then evaluate repair across interacting components.
detail: The common thread is how to evaluate and improve automated programming without mistaking plausible output for correct behavior. Each project changes the setting, but the requirement for trustworthy execution evidence remains.

LLM-ProS measures first-attempt capability on difficult algorithmic tasks. A-ProS asks whether a generator can use critic feedback and retained history to revise a failure. XLAgent moves into repositories, where a bug and its repair can span two languages and where the evaluation itself can miss part of the interaction.

I became less interested in a single score and more interested in what produces that score. A useful graph can fail to help localization; a passing test can fail to establish complete correctness. That progression motivates my proposed PhD focus on contracts, reproducible evidence and behavior-based evaluation of software agents.
questions.caution: This is a synthesis of the trajectory, not a claim that the studies share the same controlled dataset.
followups: What changed in your thinking?

questions.question: What are you working on currently?
questions.answer: My current research project is XLAgent, a manuscript under review on cross-language localization and repair. The latest evidence emphasizes strict corpus definition, null graph-localization effects and limitations of repair evaluation.
detail: I am currently working on XLAgent, a manuscript under review on cross-language bug localization and repair. It combines an empirical corpus, a cross-language dependency graph and an agent evaluation pipeline. I carried out the project with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI.

The current strict analysis retains 31 fixes from 86 confirmed cases. Graph structure recovers many modeled boundary connections but does not improve localization on the tested set. On five executable repair bugs, more two-sided edits do not establish higher correctness. Leakage and oracle limitations are central findings.

For this discussion I would use the submitted strict-result account and distinguish it from possible future experiments. The next research need is broader runnable interaction tasks and evaluation that checks both endpoints. Separately, my employment is software engineering at Therap; private production systems remain distinct from the public repositories used in the study.

questions.question: What did your RLHF work teach you?
questions.answer: I worked on code and reasoning annotation and led a ten-person pod, which exposed me to rubric quality, disagreement and consistency in evaluation.
detail: At Turing I worked on code and reasoning annotation and led a ten-person pod. That experience exposed me to rubric design, quality control and the practical difficulty of producing consistent judgments across people and tasks. It was a data and evaluation role, not a claim that I designed the company's model-training algorithms.

A label is only useful if its meaning is operational and different evaluators can apply it consistently. Disagreement can reveal an ambiguous requirement or a weak rubric rather than simply a careless annotator. That perspective connects directly to XLAgent's difficult inclusion and patch-correctness judgments.

I would build annotation examples, collect independent labels and inspect disagreement before relying on a summary metric. I would also distinguish agreement from truth, particularly for model judges. My RLHF experience informs evaluation judgment; it does not make the inference-time A-ProS loop an RLHF training method.
questions.caution: The evidence does not establish ownership of a proprietary training algorithm or measured model gains absent from the record.
followups: How would you design an annotation rubric?

questions.question: What is a strong two-minute research overview?
questions.answer: My research asks how to obtain reliable evidence for automated programming. A model can generate convincing code or a plausible patch without solving the actual task, so I have worked on execution-based evaluation and the workflow around the model.
detail: My research asks how to obtain reliable evidence for automated programming. A model can generate convincing code or a plausible patch without solving the actual task, so I have worked on execution-based evaluation and the workflow around the model.

In LLM-ProS, I built the pipeline evaluating five models on 166 World Finals problems; even the strongest first-attempt acceptance remained below ten percent. In A-ProS, I worked on orchestration, submission, logging, memory ablations and calibration for a generator-critic loop. Feedback improved observed outcomes, while the small memory solve-rate comparison remained inconclusive.

In XLAgent, I carried out a study of cross-language defects and an agent pipeline under PI supervision. The graph did not improve localization, and more two-sided edits did not establish better correctness. Those findings, along with leakage and oracle problems, motivate my PhD interest: evidence-grounded diagnosis and repair of interacting software components, with evaluation that checks the complete behavior.

questions.question: What is an LLM agent?
questions.answer: A system that repeatedly uses model outputs to choose actions, invoke tools and update task state toward an objective.
detail: An LLM agent is a system in which a model repeatedly chooses actions, uses tools and updates task state toward an objective. The model is one component; the orchestrator, permissions, memory and environment determine what it can observe and do. A single generated answer is different from that action-observation loop.

In A-ProS, a generator writes code, the judge returns evidence and a critic guides another candidate. In XLAgent, the actions include source navigation, editing and testing. The important object of evaluation is the complete workflow, including how tool output is used.

Calling a system an agent does not guarantee reliable autonomy. A tool can expose a hidden fix, a failed command can be misread or memory can retain bad advice. I therefore evaluate the trajectory and information boundary, not only the final model text. Reliability is a property of the system and task protocol.
questions.caution: Agent is a system description, not a guarantee of autonomy or intelligence.
followups: What makes a loop reliable?

questions.question: What is the difference between fault localization and repair?
questions.answer: Localization identifies relevant locations and mechanisms; repair changes code to restore intended behavior.
detail: Fault localization identifies locations and mechanisms relevant to a defect. Repair changes the program to restore intended behavior. A localizer can correctly name a file in each language while an editor still misunderstands the contract, so success in the first stage does not establish success in the second.

XLAgent measures whether reports name developer-changed files on both sides, then separately measures patch shape and resolution. The graph can have good coverage of reference locations without improving either localization or repair. Those outcomes test different parts of the proposed mechanism.

I would evaluate each stage and the end-to-end result, then inspect where the chain breaks. If localization is already near ceiling, a new navigation tool is unlikely to solve a repair failure caused by incomplete requirements or weak behavioral tests. That helps direct the next intervention toward the actual bottleneck.
questions.caution: A better intermediate metric need not improve final correctness.
followups: How can localization errors propagate?

questions.question: What is a software contract?
questions.answer: An agreement about behavior or data at an interface: input types, fields, values, errors, ordering and other assumptions both sides must share.
detail: A software contract is the agreement components rely on at an interface. It includes not just field names and types but permitted values, optionality, errors, ordering and lifecycle assumptions. The contract can be explicit in a schema or implicit in the producer and consumer implementations.

Suppose a sender serializes a numeric option as a string while the receiving client expects a number in a particular field. Each side can be locally well formed, yet the exchange is wrong. A reliable diagnosis traces the value through serialization, transport and the receiving API rather than inspecting only one file.

A graph can identify the connected endpoints, but it does not automatically explain the violated assumption. I would compare the contract evidence with a behavior reproduction and test the complete path after a change. Not every one-sided field difference is a defect; legitimate asymmetry also exists.
questions.caution: Not every textual difference is a violated contract.
followups: How can you infer implicit contracts?

questions.question: What is an evaluation oracle?
questions.answer: The mechanism used to decide whether a candidate satisfies the task, often tests plus expected outputs, wrappers and comparison rules.
detail: An oracle is the mechanism that decides whether a candidate satisfies a task. In these studies it usually consists of tests, expected outputs, wrappers, build recipes and comparison rules. A deterministic verdict is only as meaningful as that mechanism’s relationship to the intended requirement.

A broken environment or reference-specific internal assumption can reject a valid alternative. Conversely, a suite checking only one endpoint can pass while the complete interaction remains wrong. Both are important in cross-language repair because correctness is a property of the exchange, not only one component.

I would confirm fail-to-pass behavior, check the reference fix and test independent implementations against externally justified requirements. I would also separate visible feedback from hidden scoring. Oracle validation is therefore a scientific design step, not merely checking that a test command returns a status code.
questions.caution: An oracle must match the intended construct, not merely produce a deterministic answer.
followups: How do you validate an oracle?

questions.question: What is a false failure?
questions.answer: The evaluation rejects a candidate that satisfies the intended requirement, for example because configuration or implementation-coupled tests are inappropriate.
detail: A false failure occurs when an evaluator rejects a candidate that meets the intended task requirement. The defect can be in the environment, wrapper or test assumptions rather than the candidate's behavior. A failure log alone does not establish this; the attribution needs evidence.

I would hold the generated candidate fixed, identify an independently justified correction to the evaluation setup and rerun it. If the outcome changes to a legitimate pass, that supports the infrastructure explanation. For example, fixing an omitted required library link flag is different from altering the candidate algorithm.

Changing the task until a program passes is not a valid correction. Raising a timeout beyond the required efficiency limit would not make a slow solution correct. In XLAgent, developer-specific hidden names motivate a false-failure concern, but each rejected patch still needs behavioral assessment rather than blanket exemption.
questions.caution: Simply increasing a timeout until a slow program passes is not legitimate if efficiency is required.
followups: What evidence proves the candidate is valid?

questions.question: What is a false success?
questions.answer: The observed pass does not establish the intended capability, for example because solution information leaked or the tests checked only one side of an interaction.
detail: A false success is an observed pass that does not establish the capability or behavior the evaluation claims to measure. A candidate may exploit leaked solution information or satisfy an incomplete test suite while violating an unchecked requirement. The score can be mechanically accurate and scientifically misleading.

An agent reading the developer's fix is not independently deriving a repair. A Go-only hidden suite can also pass while the Python client remains wrong. Those are different mechanisms: the first concerns information access and the second concerns what the oracle covers.

I would enforce snapshot and tool isolation for the first problem and add independently justified interaction tests for the second. Passing finite tests remains bounded evidence even after those checks. The goal is not to label every success suspicious, but to match the success claim to what the protocol actually rules out.
questions.caution: Passing a finite suite remains bounded evidence even without leakage.
followups: Can tests alone prove program correctness?

questions.question: What is the difference between precision and recall?
questions.answer: Precision asks what fraction of reported positives are correct. Recall asks what fraction of all true positives were recovered.
detail: Precision is the fraction of reported positives that are correct. Recall is the fraction of all true positives that the method finds. They answer different questions, so a highly precise graph can still miss most relevant boundaries.

If a tool returns ten edges and nine are valid, precision is nine out of ten. If there are thirty real edges in the target population, recall is nine out of thirty. The tool can therefore have high precision and low recall simultaneously. This is an illustration, not another XLAgent result.

The 91.1% estimate concerns cross-language edge precision, not complete recovery. In corpus mining, reviewing every predicted positive improves confidence in retained labels but does not reveal missed negatives. To estimate recall, I need an independently known positive set or a representative audit of the material the method rejected.
questions.caution: Do not infer recall from precision without a known positive population.
followups: How would you estimate recall?

questions.question: What is a confounder?
questions.answer: A variable that changes with the intervention and could explain the observed difference, preventing a clean causal interpretation.
detail: A confounder is a variable that changes along with the intervention and could explain the observed difference. In an agent comparison, extra tokens, different feedback access or a changed backend can make an architecture look better without establishing the proposed mechanism.

A stateful workflow preserves history, which may provide useful evidence but also adds input tokens. Matching only submission counts leaves a compute difference. Likewise, running a baseline before a provider updates its model and the full system afterward mixes workflow and model-version effects.

I name the causal claim first, then match or randomize the relevant conditions and include a control that separates competing explanations. No experiment controls everything, so I report the remaining differences and keep the conclusion narrow. The purpose of a confound analysis is to improve the comparison, not merely list generic threats.
questions.caution: Listing confounders is only useful when tied to a concrete claim.
followups: Which confound is most important in your study?

questions.question: What is an ablation study?
questions.answer: Remove or replace one component while holding relevant conditions fixed to test what it contributes to a chosen outcome.
detail: An ablation removes or replaces a component while holding relevant conditions comparable to test its contribution. It should target a concrete mechanism. Removing a graph edge layer asks a different question from removing all graph tools, and clearing prior turns differs from removing the latest feedback.

I would check that the component was active and had an opportunity to influence the chosen outcome. I would also preserve tasks, backend, information and budgets as far as the claim requires. Otherwise an observed change may result from another intervention introduced by the ablation.

A component can be redundant with another or useful only on a subset of tasks. A null ablation does not prove universal uselessness. XLAgent's results therefore limit what we can attribute on the five repair tasks; they do not justify claiming all components are equivalent in every repository setting.
questions.caution: Interactions mean a component's effect can depend on the rest of the system.
followups: What if two components overlap?

questions.question: What is a percentage point versus relative improvement?
questions.answer: A change from 20% to 30% is 10 percentage points and a 50% relative improvement.
detail: A change from 20% to 30% is ten percentage points because it is the difference between two percentages. It is a 50% relative improvement because the increase of ten is half of the initial twenty. Both are valid descriptions, but they answer different questions.

In A-ProS, 19 rather than 14 accepted problems out of 47 gives about a 10.6 percentage-point advantage. The relative difference in final rates is about 35.7%. Comparing gains above a starting count of ten gives nine versus four, which produces a different ratio again.

I state the starting value, final value and denominator before summarizing an effect. Ratios become especially unstable near a small baseline, so counts help the listener assess practical size. A different arithmetic expression does not make a small or statistically inconclusive experiment more conclusive.
questions.caution: Relative percentages become unstable when the baseline is near zero.
followups: Apply this to the A-ProS ablation.

questions.question: Why use paired comparisons?
questions.answer: The same problems appear under both conditions, so the comparison preserves task difficulty and focuses on where their outcomes differ.
detail: The same problems are evaluated under both conditions, so task difficulty is shared rather than being a difference between unrelated samples. The informative cases are those where one condition succeeds and the other does not. This is particularly valuable when benchmark tasks vary greatly in difficulty.

For paired solved/unsolved outcomes, McNemar's test uses the discordant pairs. A bootstrap comparison should also preserve the task pairing when resampling. Treating the two workflow totals as independent discards useful information about which tasks overlap.

Repeated runs and multiple bugs from one repository can introduce additional dependence. I would not count every patch as an independent bug. Pairing improves comparability, but the experiment still needs enough independent tasks, a suitable endpoint and comparable information and budgets. It does not cure a weak oracle or an unrepresentative task population.
questions.caution: Repeated runs on one bug are not additional independent bug tasks.
followups: Why not use an unpaired t-test?

questions.question: What does a p-value mean?
questions.answer: Under the specified null model, it quantifies how unusual the observed test statistic or a more extreme one would be.
detail: A p-value describes how unusual the observed test statistic, or a more extreme one, would be under the specified null model. It is not the probability that the research hypothesis is true or that a result happened by chance in an unrestricted sense.

I consider the effect size, uncertainty interval, sample, assumptions and number of comparisons alongside the p-value. A result above 0.05 is not significant at that threshold, but it also does not prove no effect. It may be too imprecise to distinguish a useful improvement from zero.

The A-ProS memory p-values of 0.063 and 0.125 do not justify a conclusive acceptance benefit. I still report the observed count differences and behavioral evidence, then describe what a larger study should test. I would not call 0.063 nearly significant as a substitute for the actual inferential result.
questions.caution: Not reaching a threshold does not prove no effect.
followups: How would you report an inconclusive result?

questions.question: What does a confidence interval tell you?
questions.answer: It gives a range produced by a procedure designed to cover the target parameter at the stated long-run rate under its assumptions.
detail: A confidence interval is produced by a procedure intended to cover the target parameter at the stated long-run frequency under its assumptions. The particular interval is a useful expression of estimation uncertainty, but it is not automatically a probability distribution over the fixed parameter.

A wide interval means several effect sizes remain compatible with the method's evidence and assumptions. If a difference interval includes or touches zero, the data do not provide the same support as an interval clearly above zero. In A-ProS, the memory study’s reported intervals touch zero.

I would assess whether the interval rules out effects that matter for the research decision. Small samples and dependent observations can make a bootstrap interval unreliable, so the resampling unit matters. I prefer showing counts, paired outcomes and an interval together rather than using one number as a complete judgment of success.

questions.question: Why correct for multiple comparisons?
questions.answer: Testing many comparisons increases the chance of at least one false positive. A procedure such as Holm controls that family-wise error under its assumptions.
detail: When many comparisons are tested, the chance of at least one false positive rises. A method that produces several critic pairings or category comparisons therefore needs a declared family of tests and a procedure appropriate to the intended error control.

Holm orders the p-values and applies progressively adjusted thresholds to control family-wise error under its assumptions. The resulting conclusion can differ from looking at each raw p-value alone. In A-ProS, individual critic-pair differences do not survive the reported correction as significant findings.

I would show the raw and adjusted evidence and label exploratory comparisons separately from planned primary tests. I would not cite a favorable raw result after the corrected comparison becomes inconclusive. Multiplicity correction does not replace a good design; it addresses one specific source of overconfident inference.
questions.caution: Do not cite a raw significant result after the corrected result becomes inconclusive.
followups: Should exploratory comparisons be labeled differently?

questions.question: What is calibration versus accuracy?
questions.answer: Accuracy measures how often predictions are right; calibration measures whether expressed confidence agrees with outcome frequency.
detail: Accuracy concerns whether an output is correct. Calibration concerns whether expressed confidence matches observed outcome frequency. A critic can offer useful advice but consistently exaggerate its chance of leading to success. The ranking of usefulness and the ranking of calibration need not be identical.

If hints assigned 80% confidence lead to acceptance only 20% of the time, those hints are overconfident under that outcome definition. A lower-confidence group could be better calibrated even if it produces fewer successes overall. The relevant event must therefore be defined clearly.

A-ProS calibrates confidence against acceptance on the next generator attempt, which involves both critic and generator behavior. I would not treat that as a pure semantic hint-accuracy label. A deployable routing or abstention policy needs separate evaluation of both practical utility and uncertainty, not merely choosing the model with the lowest ECE.
questions.caution: A scalar ECE cannot fully describe every subgroup or error.
followups: How would you evaluate selective abstention?

questions.question: What is Cohen's kappa?
questions.answer: A measure of categorical agreement adjusted for the agreement expected from the raters' marginal label distributions.
detail: Cohen's kappa adjusts observed categorical agreement for the agreement expected from the raters' marginal label frequencies. It is useful when two evaluators classify inclusion, root cause or patch correctness and we want more than an unadjusted matching percentage.

In XLAgent, raters agreed strongly on whether both languages' source changed but less on whether the changes depended on each other. That distinction exposes where the rubric requires interpretation. It suggests a need for clearer examples and adjudication, not just a single overall agreement label.

Two raters can agree because they share the same misunderstanding. Kappa also depends on label prevalence and the distribution of categories. I would report raw agreement, the rubric and disagreement analysis alongside it. Agreement supports consistency of measurement; it does not establish that the labels are ground truth.
questions.caution: High agreement does not establish truth, especially for raters with shared biases.
followups: What if the label distribution is very imbalanced?

questions.question: What is runtime leakage versus training contamination?
questions.answer: Runtime leakage exposes a solution during evaluation through files, tools, history or network. Training contamination means relevant material may have entered model training beforehand.
detail: Runtime leakage occurs when the agent accesses solution-bearing information during the evaluation, such as later Git history or a scoring cache. Training contamination concerns possible prior exposure through model training. The same word contamination can obscure their different evidence and remedies.

XLAgent recorded runtime access to developer fixes through available tools and environments. Removing those channels and rerunning the tasks addresses that observed problem. It does not erase anything the model may already know from training. LLM-ProS's temporal comparison concerns that separate exposure risk.

I would isolate snapshots, network and tool outputs for runtime leakage and use prospective task collection and exposure audits for training-related concerns. Neither safeguard alone proves complete independence from all solution information. I state which threat was measured and which remains an uncertainty rather than treating a sandbox as a guarantee of uncontaminated pretraining.
questions.caution: The two threats require different evidence and safeguards.
followups: Which threat did XLAgent directly observe?

questions.question: What is fail-to-pass validation?
questions.answer: Confirm that a relevant test fails on the buggy snapshot and passes after the reference fix, under a reproducible environment.
detail: A fail-to-pass check verifies that a relevant test fails on the buggy snapshot and passes after applying the reference code fix. It establishes that the environment and suite can observe at least one known repair-related difference under the pinned setup.

Without that validation, an agent could fail because a repository cannot build or because the test never exercised the defect. The check prevents some invalid tasks from entering the executable benchmark and makes environment failures visible before the agent comparison.

The test may still depend on internal names added by the reference fix or check only one language. It can therefore be valid for the developer implementation while rejecting an independent correct repair or accepting an incomplete one. I treat fail-to-pass as necessary harness evidence, not a complete validation of the oracle's semantic coverage and implementation independence.
questions.caution: Fail-to-pass validity does not guarantee implementation-independent oracle validity.
followups: Why can a validated test still be coupled?

questions.question: What is the difference between syntax and semantics?
questions.answer: Syntax concerns valid structure; semantics concerns behavior. A patch can parse and compile yet violate a cross-language value or lifecycle contract.
detail: Syntax determines whether source follows a language's structural rules. Semantics concerns what the program does. Parsing or compilation can reject some invalid changes, but a syntactically valid program can still compute the wrong result or violate an interface contract.

Python can represent integers beyond a fixed-width Go integer's range. A value can therefore be valid on the producing side and mishandled when stored or converted on the receiving side. The source may compile in both languages even though the exchange corrupts the intended value.

A validation gate catches basic failures but cannot certify the complete interaction. I would add a boundary reproduction exercising the relevant type, range, error and optionality assumptions. This is why I separate gate acceptance, test resolution and independently assessed correctness rather than calling any compiling patch repaired.
questions.caution: Compilation alone is not enough to judge repair success.
followups: What dynamic test would expose a range bug?

questions.question: What is a baseline and what makes it fair?
questions.answer: A baseline is a comparison condition that tests an alternative explanation. Fairness requires matching the task, information, model and relevant resource budgets.
detail: A stock baseline asks whether the proposed system is practically competitive with an established approach. A matched control asks whether a particular intervention causes a difference while relevant conditions remain comparable. One comparison does not automatically answer both questions.

I would align the tasks, issue information, model version, tool access and the budget relevant to the claim. If testing a two-agent split, a single agent should not lose half the available steps merely because the architecture has fewer roles. Residual differences must still be disclosed.

XLAgent includes both a stock agent and a more closely matched single-agent condition. The latter weakens a simple attribution of two-sided edits to role separation. A good baseline is not the weakest system the method can beat; it is the condition that makes the proposed explanation testable and the practical comparison meaningful.
questions.caution: A weak baseline can exaggerate benefits, while an unmatched stronger one can obscure why results differ.
followups: Which baseline best tests a role split?

questions.question: What is a benchmark artifact release supposed to contain?
questions.answer: Task identifiers, versions, environment recipes, scoring rules, visible/hidden boundaries, run records and analysis code, with clear licenses and provenance.
detail: I would include stable task identifiers, pre-fix versions, environment recipes, visible and hidden evaluation rules, retained run records and versioned analysis. The license and provenance of source and issue text must be clear. A reader should be able to trace a reported result to the evidence that produced it.

The package should explain failed setup attempts, excluded runs, model identities and access boundaries. Keeping only successful trajectories hides important selection and cost information. Checksums and a batch registry help distinguish original evidence from later corrections.

Credentials, private data and answer-bearing artifacts must not be exposed to solving agents or unintentionally included in a public package. I would verify actual release readiness before claiming full public reproducibility. A repository link is useful, but the content and protocol determine whether another researcher can meaningfully inspect the study.
questions.caution: Actual release availability must be checked before claiming it is public.
followups: What should never be included in a public release?

questions.question: How do static and dynamic analysis complement each other?
questions.answer: Static analysis recovers possible relationships without executing the program; dynamic checks observe behavior for selected executions.
detail: Static analysis derives relationships from program structure without executing all behaviors. Dynamic analysis observes particular executions. Static tools can suggest which endpoints share a route or schema, while a reproduction can show whether a value actually crosses the boundary in the problematic way.

A static graph may guide the search toward a producer and consumer; dynamic tests can then validate their assumptions. Conversely, a runtime failure can identify where a static approximation is incomplete. Each provides a different constraint on the diagnosis rather than replacing the other.

Static matching can miss dynamic construction, and a finite execution set can miss untested paths. I would evaluate both precision and coverage and ask whether combining the evidence improves the actual repair outcome. In XLAgent, recovering relationships did not by itself establish localization benefit, which shows why representation quality and downstream utility need separate tests.
questions.caution: Neither alone generally gives complete coverage of all runtime behaviors.
followups: When is static analysis too approximate?
