questions.question: Did memory really help in A-ProS? Was it statistically significant?
questions.answer: It clearly changed behavior, but the solve-rate result is not statistically significant. On 47 matched problems, keeping history gave 19 versus 14 solved with GPT-5 and 12 versus 8 with GPT-4, about 10.6 and 8.5 percentage points. The McNemar p-values were 0.063 and 0.125, so I call that directional.
detail: On 47 problems we compared a stateful loop, which keeps history, with a stateless one that resets it. Both still got the latest feedback. GPT-5 with DeepSeek started at 10 solved and reached 19 with memory and 14 without. GPT-4 with DeepSeek started at 5 and reached 12 with memory and 8 without. So memory gained 5 and 4 tasks.

The raw exact McNemar p-values are 0.063 and 0.125, and the bootstrap intervals touch zero. At the usual 0.05 threshold that is not conclusive, and 47 tasks is a small set. The clearer effect is on repetition. Repeated failure verdicts fell from 41.8 to 11.8 percent for GPT-5, and from 40.8 to 14.2 percent for GPT-4, about 3.5 and 2.9 times lower. But that counts verdict categories, not semantic mistakes. Two wrong answers can have different causes.

I no longer use this result to argue for memory in Evident. It is a small result on a different kind of feedback, and history cannot create a missing function model or fix imprecision. History could be one ablation in a study, but the thing I actually took from A-ProS is the method: matched controls, and being honest when the numbers do not clear the bar.
questions.caution: Do not confuse this with the full ICPC result. The gain in A-ProS against a stateless loop is not a final accuracy ratio.

questions.question: Why didn't the XLAgent graph improve localization?
questions.answer: Mainly because the two sides already share a searchable name. A shell-only localizer found both developer-file sides in every run on the 12 strict localization bugs, so the graph had nothing to add. The graph was largely accurate. It just did not give the agent information it lacked.
detail: On the 12 strict localization bugs, the mean number with both sides found by file was 10.7 for full XL navigation, 11.7 for graph navigation without boundary edges, and 12.0 for shell only. So there was no measurable improvement. The graph itself was not bad. It connected both halves for 11 of 12 fixes at the boundary kinds it models, and a sampled estimate says 91.1 percent of its 8,565 cross-language edges are directly correct.

Many of these connections go through a shared name, such as a route fragment, a type or a configuration value. If you search that name in both languages, you reach the same two ends that the graph connects. So the representation can be accurate and still add nothing for this agent. A correct representation and a useful intervention are different claims.

I do not conclude that graphs are useless. The result is for this task set and setup, which also used gold-guided indexing. I would next separate bugs by how much text the two sides share, not make the graph bigger. The same lesson shapes how I think about my idea here. Extra information only counts if it beats an equal-budget control, which is why I want a blind entry arm.
questions.caution: Null result on 12 tasks. It does not show that graphs fail for all interaction bugs. XLAgent is under review.

questions.question: Why isn't a two-sided edit the same as a correct patch?
questions.answer: Two-sided only describes where a patch touches code. Correct means the interaction between the two sides actually works. On our five executable bugs, XLAgent edited both developer sides on 4.0 of 5 bugs against 2.7 for the baseline, but that did not make it more correct.
detail: A two-sided patch changes files in both languages, and in our strict metric each side includes a file the developer also changed. That tells you where the agent looked. It does not tell you whether the contract between the two sides is right. An agent can touch both files and implement the wrong contract. And a valid fix might use different files, or a justified one-sided change.

XLAgent edited both developer sides on an average of 4.0 of 5 bugs, against 2.7 for the baseline and 3.0 for the matched single agent. But only one bug, kagent 1245, was ever resolved by hidden tests. XLAgent resolved it in two of three runs and the baseline in all three. LLM judges counted 3 of 15 XLAgent patches as fully correct, against 4 for the baseline. So patch shape improved, and correctness did not.

The hidden tests have limits too, since a reference-coupled test can reject a valid fix. But that does not let me swap the harder outcome for the nicer proxy. I see the same trap in warning filtering. More warnings filtered looks like two-sided edits: it is an easy number to improve and not the same as a correct decision. That is why I would report filtered false alarms and filtered bugs separately.
questions.caution: Never treat a two-sided edit as evidence of correctness. These are five bugs with three runs each, so read them as directional.

questions.question: How does your earlier work connect to Evident?
questions.answer: The connection is the question of what counts as evidence around a fallible model, not the feedback itself. LLM-ProS measured models against a judge, A-ProS kept the final verdict outside the model, and XLAgent showed that plausible results can mislead. Evident makes a similar move in program analysis, but its feedback means something different.
detail: In all my work, the model proposes and something outside the model decides. In A-ProS, the critic and generator suggest fixes, and only the judge says what counts as fixed. Evident has the same shape: the LLM builds the harness and Eva decides. I also carry over habits, like keeping failed attempts, measuring repetition, using matched controls and checking what the agent could see. In XLAgent, 13 of 16 baseline runs had read the developers' fix before we isolated the environment.

The meaning of the signal. A judge failure says this candidate is wrong. An alarm does not say that the harness is wrong, or that the code is wrong. So a loop that worked in A-ProS cannot be copied here. Also, my small memory result does not show that history would help a formal analysis harness. I had to give up that analogy.

I can build experiment infrastructure, keep runs traceable, design fair controls and look hard at where a good-looking result might not hold. I cannot yet contribute formal methods expertise. So what I bring is complementary, and it is honest to say that the transfer is a research hypothesis and not something my earlier work has already shown.
questions.caution: A connection in method is not a result about Evident. Competitive programming and kernel warnings are different tasks.

questions.topic: Likely checks on whether you understood the paper
questions.question: What do the three validation checks do?
questions.answer: Input range checks that tainted numeric inputs keep their full type range. Sink reachability checks that Eva actually analyzed the reported operation. Path reachability looks for a gap, where an intermediate reported point is unreachable while a later one is reached. Together they target known ways of losing a bug in a harness.
detail: This has two parts. The assignment check works on the typed AST, and it requires assignments to numeric inputs to use a full-range abstract value, not a constant or a chosen range. The entry check uses Eva's values. It compares an input right after initialization and right before the selected entry, and any lost values mean generated setup code narrowed it. The paper's example is the LLM adding if (idx >= MAX) return 0; before the driver call.

Silence means nothing if the analysis never reached the code. Sink reachability checks that an abstract state reaches the reported operation. The paper's example is a generated struct with the wrong layout, so Eva loses all states before the sink. Path reachability catches a harness that reaches the sink but skips part of the reported flow. The example is setting algo.smbus_xfer to NULL, so a fallback path reaches the sink while the reported transfer path is skipped.

The paper is clear that validation does not establish that the harness preserves every relevant behavior. The input checks do not cover relational constraints, and path reachability does not show that one execution visits the points in order. Still, they matter in practice. Going from variant B to full Evident removed the one filtered bug, cut unresolved cases from five to one, and raised filtered false alarms from 99 to 102. A failed check goes back to the LLM for repair, and if that fails, the case is unresolved.
questions.caution: The checks are aimed at inadvertent construction errors. Deliberate evasion is outside the paper's scope.
followups: Why use abstract_value instead of letting the LLM choose ranges?

questions.topic: Likely checks on whether you understood the paper
questions.question: Why use abstract_value instead of letting the LLM choose ranges?
questions.answer: Because a chosen range is a place to hide an assumption. With abstract_value the LLM only says where an input is introduced, and the C type sets the range. Table 6 measures the effect: LLM-chosen inputs filtered 9 confirmed bugs, 8 of them from ranges that were too narrow, and abstract inputs reduced that to 1.
detail: In the paper's motivating example, an LLM could reason that a value normally falls between 0 and 16 and write that with Frama_C_interval. The range looks reasonable, but the real input is an attacker-controlled long, and the negative values are what trigger the bug. Eva then correctly proves the wrong program safe. With abstract_value, the LLM picks the place and the type picks the range. That also avoids mistakes with typedefs, nested structures and unions.

Variant A lets the LLM choose input values, and it filters 116 false alarms and 9 confirmed bugs. Variant B uses abstract inputs and filters 99 and 1. So the LLM's freedom bought 17 more filtered false alarms and cost 8 more filtered bugs. In the paper's reading, the same narrow restrictions that hid bugs also let Eva rule out more false alarms. That is why filtering count alone is misleading.

It applies only to numeric values. Pointers, object identities, callback bindings and string literals stay concrete, because the LLM has to build a valid context. It also does not stop generated code from narrowing a value after it is initialized. In one generated harness the initialization was correct, and a bounds check was added right after it. That is why the entry check exists.
questions.caution: abstract_value protects the range when an input is introduced. It does not prove that the rest of the harness preserves the bug.

questions.topic: Likely checks on whether you understood the paper
questions.question: Evident's accuracy is lower than BugLens. Is it worse?
questions.answer: On accuracy alone, yes: 71.0 against 76.5 percent with GPT-5.5. But accuracy is the wrong summary here, because it counts a hidden bug the same as a kept false alarm. Evident keeps 25 more false alarms than BugLens and filters 14 fewer confirmed bugs. For a warning filter, I think that is the better trade.
detail: The set has 160 false alarms and 40 confirmed bugs. If you filter every warning, you get 80 percent accuracy and hide all 40 bugs. That is higher than every system in Table 5. So accuracy on this set rewards filtering, whatever it costs. A filter should be read on two axes: how many false alarms it removes, and how many real bugs it removes.

With GPT-5.5, BugLens filters 127 false alarms and 14 confirmed bugs. Codex filters 124 and 18, and FN-aware Codex filters 123 and 11. Evident filters 102 and 0. So Evident gives up 22 to 25 false alarms against BugLens and plain Codex, and avoids 14 and 18 filtered bugs. Across all four LLMs, Evident filters no confirmed bug, while BugLens filters some with every model.

The trade is not free. 98 of 200 warnings still need inspection, and that is real human time. Whether the trade is right depends on how much a missed bug costs, and for kernel security I think that is high. It also depends on the model. With GPT-5.4 mini, BugLens filters only 28 false alarms and 4 bugs, so Evident is better on accuracy too, 59.0 against 32.0.
questions.caution: The 80 percent figure is my arithmetic from the paper's accuracy definition. It is not a system in the paper.
questions.locator: Evident v2 §6.1, Table 3, §6.3 Table 5; the 80 percent is my arithmetic

questions.topic: Likely checks on whether you understood the paper
questions.question: Does zero false negatives mean Evident is sound?
questions.answer: No, and the paper does not claim that. Eva's guarantee is about the harness, and the validation checks do not prove the harness preserved the bug. Zero of 40 is strong evidence for this set, but it is a measured result on a finite sample, not a theorem about the whole pipeline.
detail: Eva is a sound analyzer, so a clean result rules the error out in the harness. To carry that back to the original program, every error-reaching execution must also be in the harness. The paper says validation does not attempt to establish that, and that construction errors outside the checks could still filter a bug. So the soundness of Eva is not the soundness of the system.

As a rough sketch, zero misses in 40 independent cases gives a 95 percent upper bound of about 7 percent on the miss rate. The cases are not really independent, because 39 of the 40 come from one detector. And zero false negatives means little on its own, since keeping every warning also gives zero. It has to be read with the 102 filtered false alarms.

It held across four LLMs, and the design fails toward keeping a warning. The six confirmed-bug outcomes left unresolved all failed validation, so they stayed for inspection. Variant B shows the checks do real work, because the only filtered bug there is caught once validation is on. So I would call it strong empirical evidence with inspectable artifacts, which is much better than an explanation, but not a proof.
questions.caution: The 7 percent bound is my rough calculation and assumes independence, which does not fully hold.

questions.topic: Likely checks on whether you understood the paper
questions.question: What are the limitations of Evident?
questions.answer: The main ones are that validation targets construction errors that were observed, so unseen ones can still lose a bug; the checks were developed on the same 200 warnings, though with a different LLM; the evaluation covers Android drivers and taint-style warnings; and three runs per warning is a limited read on nondeterminism.
detail: Validation targets selected harness properties. It does not cover relational constraints, and reachability is checked point by point, not along one execution. Kernel models are trusted, so a wrong model could matter. And entries come from one reported call path, so other callers are outside the candidates. The paper itself states several of these in sections 4.3 and 7.

The checks were implemented and debugged on the same 200 warnings, using a different LLM, and fixed before the evaluation. So I would want to test on warnings not used in development. The set is Android kernel drivers with taint-style memory and integer warnings, and 39 of the 40 confirmed bugs come from one detector. Results may differ on other code, bug classes or backends. Labels come from earlier papers plus the authors' validation, so a wrong label could move the numbers. Three runs per warning is a limited estimate of LLM nondeterminism.

With GPT-5.5, 98 of 200 warnings remain for inspection. Serial runtime is about 10 minutes per case, mostly Eva, though cases parallelize. Weaker models leave many more unresolved. And the largest remaining causes, function models and precision, are not things a better harness prompt easily fixes. I see these as what I would examine next, not as errors. They are the normal limits of a careful study, and the paper is open about them.

So I would want to test on warnings not used in development. The set is Android kernel drivers with taint-style memory and integer warnings, and 39 of the 40 confirmed bugs come from one detector. Results may differ on other code, bug classes or backends. Labels come from earlier papers plus the authors' validation, so a wrong label could move the numbers. Three runs per warning is a limited estimate of LLM nondeterminism.

answerSections.body: With GPT-5.5, 98 of 200 warnings remain for inspection. Serial runtime is about 10 minutes per case, mostly Eva, though cases parallelize. I see these as what I would examine next, not as errors. They are the normal limits of a careful study, and the paper is open about them.

questions.question: Your first email proposed something we already do. What did you learn from that?
questions.answer: I proposed feeding harness failures back across attempts, and Evident already does that. I had missed the repair loop in Section 4.2, so I was simply wrong. I learned to find out exactly what the baseline does before proposing anything, and to check how many cases an idea can really reach.
detail: I read the paper too quickly. I saw a resemblance to A-ProS, treated a failed harness like a failed submission, and proposed something the repair loop already does. I also treated the remaining cases as if a better loop could address them, when most of them involve models or precision and not validation failures. Your questions made me go back and read it properly.

Three things. First, read the algorithm and the failure analysis, not just the abstract, and find out what the baseline already does. Second, work out the size of the target before proposing anything. Third, do not assume two kinds of feedback mean the same thing because they look alike. A judge failure and an alarm are very different signals, and I had not thought hard enough about that.

My idea became much smaller: one exit in the pipeline, at most 9 false alarms, with safety conditions that may stop it from filtering at all. I think that is a better idea, even though it is less exciting. Being corrected was useful, and I would rather be told early. If I am wrong again about what you already do, I want to know, which is why reproducing your work is my first step and not my last.

questions.question: What's your background in program analysis?
questions.answer: Honestly, it is limited. My background is LLM agents, evaluation and pipelines, not formal program analysis. I took compiler design and theory of computation, I built graph tooling over SCIP indexes in XLAgent, and I have read Evident and the Eva documentation. I have not used Frama-C or worked on the kernel.
detail: From my CSE degree I have compiler design, theory of computation and operating systems. In XLAgent I worked with per-language symbols and references from SCIP, and added cross-language edges, which is practical code indexing but not soundness-level analysis. I have also done a lot of competitive programming, so I am comfortable reading low-level code and thinking about edge cases, including integer behavior.

I have not used Frama-C or Eva. I have no kernel development experience. I have not written an abstract domain or a formal proof. My research record is in software engineering and LLM evaluation, not security. I would rather say that first than have you discover it later. What I can do now is reason about what a result establishes, and I know that is not the same as being trained in the field.

I would start with concrete work: Eva on small C programs until I can explain each alarm, then the abstract interpretation basics properly, then real driver code and your harnesses. I learn fastest by reproducing a real result and debugging why it differs. That is how I learned evaluation, through finding leakage and scoring problems in my own experiments. questions.question: Basics such as soundness, abstract interpretation, taint analysis or context sensitivity.
questions.answer: Soundness means that if the analysis says an error cannot happen, it really cannot happen in the analyzed program, usually at the cost of false alarms. Abstract interpretation gets there by computing over sets of values. Taint analysis tracks untrusted values from sources to sinks. Context sensitivity keeps different calls of a function apart instead of merging them.
detail: A sound analysis cannot stay silent on an error of the kind it checks. Completeness is the other direction: it would never give a false alarm. For real programs you cannot have both and also be fully automatic, so Eva chooses soundness. Abstract interpretation is how it works. Instead of one value, it tracks an abstraction like an interval. If i is between 0 and 7, then i plus 1 is between 1 and 8. At a merge, a simple interval domain joins 0 and 10 into 0 to 10, which also contains values no execution produces. At loops, widening jumps to a stable bound so the analysis finishes. That lost precision is where false alarms come from.

Taint analysis marks values from an untrusted source, like a user-controlled ioctl argument, and follows them through assignments and calls to a sensitive sink, like an array index or a copy size. If a value reaches a sink without being properly bounded, it reports a warning. It over-reports because it often cannot tell whether a check really bounds the value. The warnings in Evident are taint-style, from SUTURE and a CodeQL out-of-bounds detector, and Evident's job is to rule out the ones that cannot happen.

A context-insensitive analysis merges every call to a function, so facts from different callers get mixed. A context-sensitive one keeps calls apart, for example by call site. As far as I understand it, Eva analyzes a function again with the state from each call, so it keeps context as long as it starts from the right place. My helper example is the extreme case of lost context: entering at helper means no caller at all, so i is full range. Related terms are flow sensitivity for statement order, field sensitivity for struct fields and path sensitivity for correlated branches.

questions.question: Why do you want to work in this group?
questions.answer: Because your group works on the question I ended up at: how to use LLMs without trusting their judgment about program behavior. My projects kept showing that plausible output is weak evidence. Evident gives a concrete answer using program analysis, which is the skill I do not yet have and most want to build.
detail: I came to this question from the evaluation side, and your group comes from the analysis side. Evident says that if a stronger basis for a decision exists, the LLM should help make that analysis possible and not replace it. I also respect that the paper compares against your group's own earlier system, BugLens, and reports that it filters 14 confirmed bugs with GPT-5.5. Changing position in public, based on your own evidence, is how I want to do research.

I can build the experimental side: pipelines, logging, matched controls, leakage audits and careful reporting, including null results. I have also shipped software as an engineer, so I am used to systems that have to keep working. These are useful in a project where the LLM's output is a program that needs checking at every step.

I would need to learn formal analysis and kernel internals properly, and this group is where I could learn them on real problems. I am also not assuming anything about openings or funding, and I know this is a technical conversation and not a decision. What I want to find out today is whether my way of thinking would be useful to your work.

questions.question: What would you work on in your first six months?
questions.answer: First, learn by reproducing: get Frama-C and Eva running, reproduce part of Evident's published behavior, and read the residual cases. Then label those cases by cause and test the cheapest version of my idea against an equal-budget control. By six months I want a clear answer, even if the answer is that the idea does not work.
detail: Learn the tools. I would run Eva on small C programs until I can explain every alarm, then on real driver code, using the setup in the paper. Then I would reproduce a part of the published behavior, so that I understand the harnesses and the pipeline before I change anything. Along the way I would study abstract interpretation properly and read the earlier work from your group.

Label before building. For the caller-constraint cases, I would record which entry was used, whether the guard is on the call witness, whether a higher entry is possible, and whether it times out. That labeling alone could answer whether my idea has a target. If it does not, I would move to what the data suggests, and precision may be the better direction. I would discuss that with you before spending more time.

If the idea survives, I would build the equal-budget blind arm and the guided arm with the negative controls, run them, and audit each newly filtered case by hand. Then I would write up the result, even if it is null. This is only my plan from outside the group. In practice I would work on what the group needs most, and I would expect it to change after the first month.

questions.question: Can you tell me about your research journey?
questions.answer: My research asks how we can know that AI-written code really works. I started by testing models on very hard contest problems. Then I added feedback so models could learn from failures. Then I moved to real bugs between two programming languages. Each project made me more careful about what a good result really means.
detail:
Sure. My name is Md Sifat Hossain. I studied Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Dhaka, and now I work as a software engineer at Therap. I also continue my research with the Data Mining Research Lab at the University of Dhaka, with my supervisor Md. Fahim Arefin.

My journey started with competitive programming. I have solved more than a thousand problems, and I have competed at the ICPC Dhaka Regional. So I know how hard a contest problem can be. One small mistake, and the whole solution fails.

When large language models became good at writing code, I wanted to test them in that hard setting. That became my first project, LLM-ProS. We took 166 problems from the ICPC World Finals, from 2011 to 2024. I built the pipeline. It collected the problems, cleaned them and put them in one format. Five models then got one attempt on each problem, and I sent the solutions to a real judge on Codeforces Gym. Nobody decided by reading the code. The judge decided.

The result was very clear. The best model, o1-mini, solved only 16 of the 166 problems, about 9.6 percent. Three of the five models solved none. This paper appeared at the LLM4Code workshop at ICSE 2025. So models could write code that looked right, but most of it failed. That gave me my next question. If the first attempt fails, can the model learn from the failure?

My undergraduate thesis looked at this idea, and A-ProS then studied it at a much larger scale. In A-ProS we split the work into two roles. One model, the generator, writes the code. If the judge rejects it, a second model, the critic, reads the problem, the failed code and the judge's result. The critic explains what went wrong. Then the generator tries again. Each problem gets one first attempt and up to three more rounds.

We tested two generators with three critics on 367 problems. My part was the system around the models. I designed the pipeline that moves each problem through these steps. I built the browser automation that submits code to Codeforces and reads the verdict. I built a SQLite database that records every attempt, so we could study what happened, not only the final score. I also ran the memory study and the calibration study.

Feedback helped a lot. On the 167 ICPC problems, GPT-5 went from 39 solved to between 85 and 90. GPT-4 went from 15 to between 31 and 38. But I want to be careful here. We also tested whether keeping memory between rounds really helped. On 47 problems the version with memory solved more, but the difference was not statistically significant. The clear effect was that models repeated the same kind of failure much less. We also found that critics were not well calibrated. So a confident explanation is not the same as a correct one. This work was published in ACM TOSEM in 2026, and I share equal contribution with Anika Tabassum.

Contest problems are clean, but real software is not. In real projects, two languages often work together. For example, a Go service sends data to a Python client. A bug can sit between them, so each side looks fine alone. That is my third project, XLAgent, which is under review. I carried it out independently, with Md. Fahim Arefin as the PI.

First I studied these bugs. I looked at 145 repositories that use Java with TypeScript, or Python with Go. We confirmed 86 cross-language bug fixes, and 31 passed a strict test: both languages really had to change because of how they work together. The biggest cause was a mismatch in the contract between the two sides. In simple words, the two sides disagree about the data they exchange.

Then I built a graph that connects code across the two languages, and an agent that finds a bug and then fixes it. The hope was that the graph would help a lot. It did not. The graph was mostly correct, but a simple agent with only shell search, like grep, found both sides in every run, because the two sides share a name. On five bugs that we could run, my agent edited both languages more often, but its fixes were not more correct. I also found a serious problem in the evaluation. Before I isolated the environment, 13 of 16 baseline runs had read the developers' real fix, for example from Git history. So I rebuilt the setup and ran the experiments again.

When I look back, each project made me more careful. First I asked, can the model solve it? Then I asked, can feedback help? Then I had to ask, how do we even know the fix is correct? That last question is what I care about now. For my PhD, I want to study how to tell a fix that only looks right from a fix that really works. To do that, I want to learn program analysis and better experiment design. I am happy to go deeper into any of these projects.
questions.caution: 39 to 90 is out of 167 ICPC problems, not all 367. Memory results are not statistically significant. Two-sided edits are not correctness. XLAgent is under review, so never say it is accepted.

answerSections.heading: The three projects
answerSections.body:
I have done three projects. The first is LLM-ProS. I built a pipeline that tested five models on 166 ICPC World Finals problems, using a real judge. The best model solved fewer than ten percent.

The second is A-ProS. We added a second model that reads the failure and gives a hint, and then the first model tries again. On 167 ICPC problems, GPT-5 went from 39 solved to between 85 and 90. I built the pipeline, the submission system and the logging, and I ran the memory and calibration studies.

The third is XLAgent, which is under review. I studied bugs that sit between two programming languages, and I built a graph and an agent to find and fix them.

answerSections.heading: What I learned
answerSections.body:
XLAgent taught me the most, because many of its results were negative. The graph did not help the agent find bugs, because simple text search was already enough. More patches touched both languages, but they were not more correct. I also found that 13 of 16 baseline runs had read the real fix before I isolated the environment.

So now I care most about measurement. For my PhD, I want to study how to check that a software agent really fixed something, and not only that the result looks good.

questions.question: What work have you done so far?
questions.answer: I have done three research projects and an undergraduate thesis. Two papers are published, LLM-ProS and A-ProS, and XLAgent is under review. I also work as a software engineer at Therap, and I have a strong competitive programming background.
detail:
I have done three research projects. LLM-ProS is a workshop paper from the LLM4Code workshop at ICSE 2025. It tests five models on ICPC World Finals problems. A-ProS is a journal paper in ACM TOSEM in 2026. It is a loop where one model writes code and another model helps fix it. XLAgent is my current project, and it is under review. It looks at bugs that sit between two programming languages.

I also wrote an undergraduate thesis with Md. Fahim Arefin as my advisor. Its title is A Hybrid LLM Feedback Framework for Automated Competitive Programming Workflows. It tested a pipeline where several models work together to find and fix errors, with Codeforces as the check.

In these projects, I do the hands-on research work. I build datasets. I write scrapers and browser automation. I connect models, judges and tools into one pipeline. I log every step in a database, so that the results can be checked later. Then I run the experiments and analyze the results, including controlled comparisons and basic statistics. In XLAgent I also built code indexing tools and an isolated test environment.

I am also a software engineer at Therap, where I work on a healthcare software system with Java, Spring and Hibernate. So I know what it means to change real code safely. I also worked at Turing on code and reasoning annotation, and I led a team of ten people there. That taught me how hard it is to judge code quality in a consistent way.

And I come from competitive programming. I have solved more than a thousand problems, and I have competed at the ICPC Dhaka Regional. All of this gives me a strong practical base. What I still need is deeper training in research methods and program analysis.

questions.question: Can you explain LLM-ProS and what you did in it?
questions.answer: LLM-ProS tested five large language models on 166 ICPC World Finals problems, with one attempt each and a real judge. I built the pipeline that collected the problems and submitted the solutions, and I analyzed the results. The best model solved only 16 problems.
detail:
LLM-ProS is my first paper. It appeared at the LLM4Code workshop at ICSE 2025. The question was simple. How well can large language models solve very hard programming problems on the first try?

We chose ICPC World Finals problems for a reason. These problems are hard. A solution needs the right algorithm and correct code. It must handle edge cases, and it must stay inside the time and memory limits. So code can look very good and still fail. That is why a real judge is a much stronger test than a person reading the code, or another model saying it looks fine.

My part was the evaluation pipeline, so let me walk you through it. First, I collected 166 World Finals problems, from 2011 to 2024, from the official ICPC website. Each problem has a statement, input and output rules, sample tests and limits.

Second, I cleaned each problem and put it into one standard format, so every model received the problem in the same way. This step matters. If I lose one rule while cleaning, then I am testing a different problem.

Third, five models generated solutions: GPT-4o, Mistral Large, Llama 3.1 405B, o1-mini and o1-preview. Each model got one attempt on each problem. Fourth, I built the automatic submission to Codeforces Gym, so every solution got a real verdict, such as accepted, wrong answer, time limit exceeded, runtime error or compile error. Finally, I analyzed those verdicts, and also the error types and the use of time and memory.

The result was clear. o1-mini solved 16 of the 166 problems, which is 9.64 percent. o1-preview solved 15. The other three models solved none in this setting. Most of the o1-mini failures, 124 of them, were wrong answers.

I want to be honest about what this does not show. The o1 models did better, but this study cannot prove that chain-of-thought reasoning was the reason. We also compared results by year, which raises the question of whether models had seen older problems during training. But we cannot prove that either.

This project taught me two things. First, the pipeline is part of the research. If it has a mistake, the result is wrong. Second, the low score gave me my next question. If most first attempts fail, can a model use the failure to do better? That question became A-ProS.
questions.caution: A workshop paper, not the ICSE main track. Do not claim that chain-of-thought caused the gap, or that contamination was proved.
questions.locator: LLM-ProS §III, Table II, §IV; author contribution record

questions.question: Can you explain A-ProS and what you did in it?
questions.answer: A-ProS is a loop where one model writes code, a judge tests it, and a second model explains the failure so the first model can try again. We tested six model pairs on 367 problems. I built the pipeline, the submission system and the logging, and I ran the memory and calibration studies.
detail:
A-ProS is my journal paper, published in ACM TOSEM in 2026. I share equal contribution with Anika Tabassum. After LLM-ProS, we knew that most first attempts fail. So we asked, what happens after a failure?

The main idea is to split the work into two roles. One model, the generator, writes a C++ solution. We used GPT-4 and GPT-5. A real judge tests it. If it fails, another model, the critic, looks at the problem, the failed code and the judge's result, and it explains what went wrong. We used three critics: Codestral, Llama 3.3 and DeepSeek-R1. The generator then tries again, and it can see the history of earlier attempts.

Each problem gets one first attempt and up to three more rounds, so four submissions at most. Two generators and three critics give six workflows. We tested them on 367 problems: 167 from the ICPC World Finals and 200 from Codeforces.

My work was mainly the system that makes this loop run, and the studies on top of it. I designed the orchestration pipeline. It moves each problem through the steps: get the problem, generate code, submit it, read the verdict, ask the critic and try again.

I built the browser automation that submits the code to Codeforces and waits for the final verdict. Browser automation can break easily, so it needed time limits and backup steps. I also built the SQLite logging. It links each problem, code version, hint and verdict. This sounds simple, but it made the analysis possible. Without it, we would only have a final score, and we could not study how a run developed.

I also ran two studies. The first was the memory study. On 47 problems, I compared the normal loop with a version that clears its memory before each round, but still gets the latest failure and hint. The second was the calibration study. We asked each critic how confident it was, and compared that with whether the next attempt was accepted.

Feedback helped a lot. On ICPC, GPT-5 workflows went from 39 accepted to between 85 and 90, out of 167. GPT-4 workflows went from 15 to between 31 and 38. On Codeforces, out of 200, GPT-5 workflows reached 73 to 82, and GPT-4 workflows reached 42 to 52. DeepSeek-R1 gave the best numbers, but the differences between critics were not significant after correction.

I am careful about the memory result. With memory, GPT-5 solved 19 against 14, and GPT-4 solved 12 against 8. But the p-values were 0.063 and 0.125, so it is not statistically significant. The clearer effect was on repetition. With GPT-5, repeated failure verdicts were about 12 percent with memory, against about 42 percent without it. The calibration study showed that critics were not well calibrated, so you should not trust a hint only because a model sounds sure.

There is also one limit on the word autonomous. For some ICPC problems, detailed test information had to be collected by hand. My main lesson is that a model's explanation is only a suggestion. The judge decides. That idea stayed with me in my later work.
questions.caution: 39 to 90 is out of 167, not 367. A gain ratio is not a final accuracy ratio. Memory solve-rate results are not statistically significant, and repeated verdicts are not the same as repeated semantic mistakes.

questions.question: Can you explain XLAgent and what you did in it?
questions.answer: XLAgent studies bugs that sit between two programming languages, and tests an agent that tries to find and fix them. I carried out the project with Md. Fahim Arefin as PI. The graph did not improve bug finding, and patches that touched both languages were not more correct. It is under review.
detail:
XLAgent is my current project, and it is under review. I carried it out independently, with Md. Fahim Arefin as the PI.

Real software often uses two languages. For example, a Go service may send data to a Python client. The two sides talk through things like web routes, JSON fields or gRPC messages. A compiler checks each language alone, so it may not see a mismatch between them. Each side can look correct, and the bug is between them.

So first I wanted to understand these bugs. I looked at 145 repositories that use Java with TypeScript, or Python with Go. They had 1,206 merged pull requests that changed both languages. From these we confirmed 86 cross-language bug fixes. Then we applied a strict rule: both languages must really need to change because of how they work together. Only 31 passed. The biggest cause was a contract or schema mismatch, which means the two sides disagree about the data they exchange. That was 11 of the 31.

Then I built two main things. The first is a graph that connects code across languages. It starts from per-language code indexes made with SCIP. Then it adds links for things like routes, headers, shared data types and protobuf services. There are 9,605 of these boundary links. From a labeled sample, we estimate that about 91 percent of the cross-language links are correct.

The second is the agent, and it works in steps. A read-only agent finds the related code on both sides. Next, a contract step checks what the two sides agree on and suggests possible fixes. Then an editing agent writes the patch. A validation gate checks for new basic errors, and visible tests can start another round. The hidden tests are only used for the final score, so the agent cannot see them. I also built the evaluation setup around all of this.

The results were mostly not what we hoped for, and that is why I find them useful. First, the graph did not improve bug finding. On 12 bugs, a simple agent with only shell search, like grep, found both sides in every run. The two sides share a name, so search reaches the same code. Second, on five bugs that we could run, my system edited the developers' files on both sides more often, 4.0 of 5 bugs against 2.7 for the baseline. But correctness did not improve. Hidden tests only ever passed on one bug, and the baseline passed it more often, in all three runs against two.

I also found a serious problem in the evaluation. Before I isolated the environment, 13 of 16 baseline runs had read the developers' real fix or later information, for example from Git history. So a run could look successful only because it found the answer. I added isolation and auditing, and I ran the experiments again. Later I found a second leak through the files of the graph tool, and I replaced those runs too.

The tests also have limits. In one bug, a patch could pass the test on the Go side and still handle the Python side wrongly. So my main lesson is this. A result that looks good is not enough. We need a way to check that the whole interaction really works. That is the problem I want to work on next.
questions.caution: Under review, so do not name a venue or claim acceptance. Use only the strict numbers. 86 is confirmed fixes and 31 is the strict set. Two-sided edits are not correctness.
questions.locator: XLAgent strict 21 October revision, RQ1 to RQ5; leakage audit; author ownership record

questions.question: How did one project lead to the next?
questions.answer: Each project came from the limit of the one before it. LLM-ProS showed that most first attempts fail, so A-ProS asked whether feedback helps. A-ProS used clean contest problems, so XLAgent moved to real software. XLAgent then showed that our measurements can mislead us, and that is what I want to study next.
detail: Each project came from the limit of the one before it. LLM-ProS measured one thing: can a model solve a hard problem on the first try? Mostly, it could not. But a first attempt is not how people work. When my code fails in a contest, I read the verdict and I try again. So the natural next question was whether a model can do the same.

That became A-ProS, where a critic explains the failure and the model tries again. It worked well on contest problems. But contest problems are clean. One program, clear rules and a judge that tests everything. Real software is not like that. As a software engineer, I see that one part can look correct while the full path is broken, because another part reads the data differently. So I moved to real repositories and to bugs between two languages. That became XLAgent.

In the first two projects, the judge told us clearly what passed. In XLAgent there is no perfect judge. Tests can check only one side, and agents can find the real answer by accident. So my focus changed. I started with the question, how good is the model? Now my question is, how do we know the result is real? That is the direction I want to continue in a PhD.
questions.caution: The papers use different models and tasks. Do not subtract their success rates and call the difference an effect of A-ProS.

I also ran the memory study and the critic calibration analysis. Anika Tabassum and I share equal contribution, so I always give that credit clearly.

answerSections.heading: XLAgent, and how I give credit
answerSections.body:
In XLAgent, I carried out the project independently, with Md. Fahim Arefin as the PI. I did the repository mining, the graph tooling, the localization and editing pipeline and the evaluation setup. I also investigated the leakage and the problems with the tests.

When I talk about my work, I say I for the parts I built or ran, and we for the joint design and the paper's conclusions. Independent work does not mean nobody helped me. I had supervision and review. My claim is simple: I can explain every step of what I built, and its limits.

speech.label: My own part in each project
speech.cue: "What exactly did you do yourself?" "What was your role?"

questions.question: What have you learned from your research so far?
questions.answer: I learned three things. A result that looks good is not proof. A negative result is still useful if it is honest. And the evaluation is part of the research, so it needs as much care as the system. Now I want to learn how to measure these things properly.
detail: The first thing I learned is that a good-looking result is not proof. In LLM-ProS, code that looked right failed in front of a real judge. In A-ProS, a critic could sound sure and still be wrong. In XLAgent, a patch could touch both languages and still not fix the bug. So now, when I see a good number, my first question is, what does this number really show?

The second thing is that a negative result is still useful, if it is honest. In XLAgent, the graph did not improve bug finding. I could have tried to hide that behind other numbers, but I reported it. Understanding why it failed was more useful, because it showed that text search was already enough. The memory result in A-ProS was similar. It was not statistically significant, so I do not say that it was.

The third thing is that the evaluation is part of the research. Finding that 13 of 16 baseline runs had read the real fix changed how I think. If the setup is wrong, every number after it is wrong too. So I now spend real time checking the setup before I trust the result.

What I still need is deeper training. I want to learn program analysis, statistics and experiment design properly. That is why I want to do a PhD. I do not only want to build systems that look like they work. I want to learn how to show that they do.
questions.caution: A lesson from these projects is not a general result about all agents or all software.

glossary.definition: A controlled removal or replacement of a component to investigate its contribution.
A model-driven system that takes actions through tools and maintains task state.
The route, schema, header, RPC or other object tying two language-side sites together.
Agreement between expressed confidence and observed outcome frequency.
Contest infrastructure used to judge generated solutions in the first two projects.
Shared assumptions about data, behavior, errors or ordering at an interface.
In XLAgent, a patch changing non-test code in only one counted language.
Expected Calibration Error: a weighted absolute gap between confidence and outcome frequencies.
A test fails on the buggy snapshot and passes after the reference fix.
An evaluation rejection that does not reflect violation of the intended requirement.
An apparent evaluation pass that does not establish the intended capability.
An interface connecting code across language runtimes, such as a mobile bridge.
The A-ProS role responsible for producing the next candidate solution.
The A-ProS role responsible for diagnosing a failure and proposing a debugging hint.
The developer reference fix used by an evaluator, which must stay hidden from an agent.
Choosing indexed modules with knowledge of the developer fix; an XLAgent limitation.
RPC infrastructure with protobuf service and message definitions as explicit shared mediators.
The code and environment that prepare, run, observe and score an experiment.
An oracle requiring reference-specific internal details rather than just task behavior.
Categorical agreement adjusted for agreement expected from the raters' label distributions.
Identifying source locations relevant to a defect before changing code.
A comparison that holds relevant model, information and resource conditions constant.
A paired binary-outcome test based on discordant task results.
No detected effect under a particular experiment; not automatic proof of equivalence.
The mechanism that decides whether a candidate satisfies the task.
Measured success on the first generated candidate under a specified protocol.
The arithmetic difference between two percentages.
The fraction of retrieved or predicted positives that are correct.
The fraction of all true positives that are retrieved.
Previously working behavior that fails after a change.
A running agent accessing solution-bearing evidence meant to be hidden.
Structured symbols and references used for semantic code navigation.
Preserves prior conversation turns for the current task.
Clears prior turns; in the A-ProS paper the latest verdict and hint remain in the current prompt.
An XLAgent defect repair needing interacting non-test source changes in both languages.
Possible pretraining exposure to a benchmark task or solution.
Syntax parsing used for structure, source ranges and extraction rules.
In the strict XLAgent metric, changes a developer-changed non-test file in each language.
In A-ProS, total judge submissions divided by accepted solutions, including failed tasks.
Computes over manageable sets of possible states. An over-approximation can retain alarms for infeasible behaviors.
A model includes the relevant concrete behaviors and may include extra ones. Extra behaviors can create conservative alarms.
A model omits some relevant concrete behaviors. A safe result can then fail to justify safety of the original program.
Original code and state before a helper or callback that may establish constraints relevant to an analysis.
The source and justification of a condition used in a model, including its version and context coverage.
A conclusion about the generated context, which requires a separate preservation argument to transfer to the original program.
An error remains possible in the analysis; a feasible concrete defect is not necessarily confirmed.
Whether a feasible execution reaches the reported operation in a state violating the property.
A deliberately chosen case on which a proposed improvement must not produce the favorable outcome, such as an unsafe alternate caller.
Which warning-relevant feasible caller, object and environmental situations a harness represents.
A justified relation between analysis conclusions and the modeled program under explicit assumptions; empirical zero-error observations are not a theorem.
Turning a title term such as reliable or autonomous into a measurable property, protocol and boundary.
